communities.notes: Actually a large, long-lived forum with about 35,000 accounts, an owner, a dozen moderators and a dense rulebook in a pinned thread. The description gives no hint of any of it.

communities.name: Hearing Loss Café

description.purpose: For adults in Taipei and nearby with hearing loss, and their family members. We meet once a month in a quiet café with good lighting so we can lip-read, and in this LINE group we share tips on hearing aids, cochlear implants, captioning apps, workplace rights and subsidies.
description.culture: Use whatever works for you: speaking, sign, writing, typing. Everyone is patient here. When you post a video, please add captions or a summary.

communities.notes: About 200 members, mostly people who lost hearing later in life. Run by a retired teacher and an audiologist's assistant. Deaf signers who joined found it oriented to hearing aids and lip-reading, and a few have left.

communities.name: Fiber Commons Cooperative

description.purpose:
Fiber Commons is a member-owned broadband cooperative bringing fiber internet to the towns of the Northeast Kingdom that the big providers decided weren't worth it. Since we lit our first connection in 2019, we've built over 600 miles of fiber and now serve about 1,100 member households and businesses.

This forum is for members. Use it to:
- Report outages and get status updates (staff post here first).
- Ask questions about your service, billing or equipment.
- Discuss co-op business: budgets, build-out priorities, rates, board decisions.
- Help your neighbors with router setup and Wi-Fi.

How the co-op is governed:
- Every household or business that subscribes is a member with one vote, no matter what plan you have.
- Members elect a nine-person board at the Annual Meeting in May. Board members serve staggered three-year terms.
- The board hires the general manager, approves the budget and sets rates. Board meetings are monthly and open to members, except for personnel and legal matters. Minutes are posted here.
- Any member can put a motion on the Annual Meeting agenda with 25 member signatures.
- Surplus revenue goes back into build-out or is returned to members as capital credits.

Forum guidelines: be civil. Criticise decisions, not people, and especially not our staff, who are your neighbors. No sales or political campaigning. Moderated by staff and two volunteer members.

About the February outage: as most of you know, a contractor cut the main line near Lyndonville and some members were offline for almost three days in subzero weather. The board has published a full report. Many members have asked why we didn't have a redundant route, and why communication was so slow. Both are fair questions. The board is proposing to accelerate the redundancy project, which would require a modest rate increase, and will hold a special member meeting in April to discuss it before any vote.
description.culture: We're neighbors who built this together. We expect a lot from the co-op, and the co-op expects members to show up.

communities.notes: Strong formal democracy, but turnout at meetings is around 5%, and the forum is dominated by a vocal handful. The outage and proposed rate increase have energised people who had never engaged before, some of them angry.

communities.name: Ravenhurst & District Model Railway Club

description.purpose: Since January, the Ravenhurst Model Railway Society and the Ellesby & District Railway Modellers have joined together as one club. We now meet at the Ellesby clubrooms on Tuesday and Friday evenings, with the Ravenhurst layout moving there in March. Members of both old clubs are automatically members. All gauges, all eras, all skill levels.
description.culture: We know change isn't easy, and both clubs had their own ways of doing things. A joint interim committee will run things until the first AGM in June, where a new constitution will be voted on. Please be patient with each other, and if you have concerns, talk to any committee member.

communities.notes: About 70 members, mostly retired men. The merger was driven by falling membership and the loss of Ravenhurst's rooms. The two clubs had very different cultures (one formal, one chaotic), and arguments about whose layout gets space are proxies for who's in charge.

communities.name: Polish Mums in Dublin

description.purpose: Group for Polish mums in Dublin and nearby: schools, doctors, playdates, and swaps.
description.culture: Help each other, no hate.

communities.notes: About 6,000 members, run by two admins who approve every post. Mostly practical help, with frequent clashes over vaccination and Polish politics that the admins shut down.

communities.name: Ask a Geologist

description.purpose: The listener Discord for Ask a Geologist, the podcast about rocks, volcanoes, earthquakes and deep time. Share photos in #what-rock-is-this, suggest questions for upcoming episodes, talk about the latest eruption, and plan field trips with other listeners.
description.culture: Curiosity is the only requirement. Real geologists hang out here, so be ready for 'well, technically...'. No crystal healing claims in science channels, please; there's #woo-free-zone for a reason.

communities.notes: About 1,800 members. The host pops in a couple of times a week; three listener mods run it. A few professional geologists answer most questions, and amateurs sometimes feel talked down to.

communities.name: Harbor Grants DAO

description.purpose:
Harbor Grants funds open-source software, public research and community infrastructure that the market doesn't pay for. Since 2022 we've distributed grants to more than 300 projects. HARBOR token holders govern the treasury: they elect the grants committee, approve budgets, and vote on major proposals.

How governance works (current process):
1. Ideas start as a post in the Ideas category on Discourse, with at least 7 days of discussion.
2. Formal proposals use the HIP (Harbor Improvement Proposal) template and need sponsorship by a delegate holding at least 0.5% of voting power.
3. Voting runs for 5 days on Snapshot. Quorum is 4% of circulating supply; a simple majority passes most proposals, and 66% is needed for treasury changes above 1M.
4. Passed proposals are executed by the 5-of-9 multisig, whose signers are elected annually.

Grants: the grants committee (5 elected members) runs quarterly rounds, publishes its reasoning for every decision, and is reviewed by token holders twice a year.

What happened in September: HIP-118 proposed moving 40% of the treasury into a liquidity program run by an outside protocol. Discussion was overwhelmingly negative, but a single wallet that acquired a large number of tokens days before the vote, plus two delegates, passed it with 52%. The multisig signers declined to execute it, citing their duty to protect the DAO, which some members praised and others called a betrayal of on-chain governance.

Where we are now: we've paused major treasury votes and opened a 60-day Governance Review. Proposals on the table include a time-lock on newly acquired tokens, a 'veto council' of long-standing contributors, and quadratic voting for grants. Everyone is invited to take part in the Review threads and the weekly community calls.
description.culture: Builders funding builders. We believe in public goods and in transparent decision-making, even when it's messy. Please argue in good faith; assume people care about the DAO even when they disagree with you.

communities.notes: About 6,000 token holders, with a few hundred who participate. The September vote exposed that 'token holders decide' and 'the community decides' are not the same thing, and the multisig's refusal showed where power actually sits.

communities.name: Lola's Plant Swaps

description.purpose: My Telegram channel for plant friends around Metro Manila! I post cuttings and pups I have to give away or swap, plant care tips that actually work in our humidity, and the occasional plant haul. If you want something, comment and I'll reply. Meetups at my place in Marikina every other Saturday.
description.culture: First come first served, but I give priority to people who haven't gotten anything yet. No reselling my free cuttings please! 🌿

communities.notes: About 120 subscribers, mostly women in their 20s–40s. Lola (her nickname, not 'grandma') decides everything; the channel only allows comments, and the real community happens at her Saturday meetups.

communities.name: Patel & Sons

description.purpose: Family group. Shop rota, deliveries, and dinner at Ba's on Sunday.

communities.notes: Eleven family members who also run a convenience shop together. Who's on the till and whose turn it is to host dinner get decided in the same chat, so business disagreements and family tensions blur into each other, and Dad's word is final on both.

communities.name: Exchange Crew 2019

description.purpose: The group chat from our exchange semester in Utrecht, 2019. Fourteen of us from nine countries. Now it's birthday messages, photos from each other's weddings, and endless plans for a reunion that we will DEFINITELY make happen this time.
description.culture: No time zone shaming. Lurking allowed. Reply to the reunion poll, Kenji.

communities.notes: Fourteen friends in nine countries. No real organiser; three people carry the chat while most react occasionally, and the reunion has been planned and cancelled three times.

communities.name: Ōtautahi Mutual Aid

description.purpose:
Ōtautahi Mutual Aid is neighbours helping neighbours in Christchurch. We started in the weeks after the 2011 earthquake, when the official help wasn't reaching the eastern suburbs fast enough, and people in Aranui, New Brighton and Dallington organised themselves to get water, food and portaloos to whoever needed them. We never really stopped. During Covid we did grocery runs; now we mostly do food parcels, lifts to appointments, moving help, and a winter firewood and blanket drive.

How to ask for help: post in the Facebook group or message the WhatsApp request line. Say what you need, roughly where you are, and when. You don't need to explain why. A volunteer will reply or message you privately. If it's an emergency, call 111 first.

How to help: comment on a request or message the person directly. If you take a request, follow through or say you can't, so it doesn't fall through the cracks. Our coordinators (currently Hemi, Sarah, and Ana) keep an eye on requests that haven't been picked up.

Some agreements:
- This is mutual aid, not charity. Everyone gives and receives. No one is 'the needy' and no one is 'the helpers'.
- Don't share anyone's request, address or story outside the group.
- No judging requests. If someone asks for food, they get food.
- No selling, no political campaigning, no church recruitment.
- Volunteers are never alone in someone's home for the first time; bring a buddy.

The honest bit: we're tired. Requests have doubled in the last two years with the cost of living, and the same 20 or 30 people do most of the work. Two of our longtime coordinators stepped back this winter because of burnout. We've talked about applying for funding or partnering with a social service agency, but many of us worry that would turn us into an organisation with forms and eligibility rules, which is exactly what we started as an alternative to. We're having a hui about it next month. Come, have a cup of tea and tell us what you think.
description.culture: Kia ora. Manaakitanga: we look after people. Be kind, be reliable, be humble.

communities.notes: About 1,400 members, with a core of 20–30 active volunteers who are mostly Māori and Pākehā women in the eastern suburbs. Growing demand is pushing them toward formalising, which threatens the identity that keeps volunteers motivated.

communities.name: Gdańsk Citizens' Assembly on Climate

description.purpose: The online space for members of the Gdańsk Citizens' Assembly on climate adaptation. 90 residents, selected by random draw to reflect the city by age, gender, district and education, meet over six weekends to hear from experts, deliberate, and vote on recommendations. Recommendations with at least 80% support are binding on the mayor. Observers can follow along and submit comments.
description.culture: Every member's voice counts equally, whether you're 17 or 87. Facilitators keep discussions fair. Experts inform; they don't decide. Please keep deliberations respectful, and keep members' personal details private.

communities.notes: Members were chosen by lottery, and an independent coordinating team, not the city, runs the process. Observers and activist groups watch closely and some try to lobby members privately, which the rules forbid.

communities.name: Hotel Aurora Housekeeping

description.purpose: Daily room assignments, shift changes and supply requests for the housekeeping team.

communities.notes: 22 room attendants and two supervisors at a Cancún resort. Supervisors post assignments at 7am; the attendants also have their own separate chat where they trade tips about difficult guests and managers.

communities.name: Data Journalists Africa

description.purpose: A Slack for journalists, editors, developers and researchers doing data-driven reporting in Africa. Find datasets, get help with scraping and visualisation, ask how to file access-to-information requests in different countries, share your stories, and hear about fellowships and training.
description.culture: Generous and practical. Share what you know, credit others' work, and protect sources: never post anything that could identify a vulnerable source. English and French welcome.

communities.notes: About 900 members, started by a media development NGO that still pays a community manager. Anglophone members dominate, and francophone members have asked repeatedly for more attention.

communities.name: Intro to Seaweed Farming

description.purpose:
Welcome to the discussion forum for Intro to Seaweed Farming, a free online course from the Ocean Livelihoods Institute. Over eight modules, you'll learn the basics of seaweed biology, site selection, rope and raft systems, harvesting, drying and markets, with case studies from Zanzibar, the Philippines, Indonesia, Chile and Scotland.

Until this year, the course ran in fixed cohorts twice a year, with live sessions, teaching assistants and assignments. From this year, the course is self-paced: you can start any time, and all materials stay open. The forum stays open too, and has become the main way learners help each other.

How to use the forum:
- Each module has a discussion board. Post questions there.
- Introduce yourself in Introductions: where you are, and whether you farm already.
- The Farmers' Corner is a space for working farmers to share practical experience, and is now the busiest part of the forum.
- Course staff check the forum weekly, rather than daily as during cohorts. Community TAs, volunteers from earlier cohorts, help answer questions.

Forum rules:
- Be respectful; learners come from very different backgrounds, from university students to farmers who have worked the sea for 30 years.
- No selling equipment or seed stock, except in the Marketplace board.
- Don't post others' contact details.

We know the switch to self-paced has changed things. Some learners miss the deadlines and live sessions, and some farmers have asked if the Farmers' Corner could become a permanent network independent of the course. We're discussing this with the community TAs and would love to hear your thoughts in the 'Future of this forum' thread.
description.culture: Practical, international and respectful of local knowledge. Farmers often know more than the textbook, and we want to hear from them.

communities.notes: About 12,000 registered learners, a few hundred active. It started as a class but is turning into a professional network for farmers, while the Institute still controls the platform and the rules.

communities.name: Plastic-Free Bali

description.purpose: We're working to free Bali from single-use plastic. We organise weekly beach and river cleanups, run a pledge program for warungs, cafés and hotels, campaign for enforcement of the provincial plastic ban, and teach waste sorting in schools. Join a cleanup, sign your business up, or volunteer with our school team.
description.culture: Action over talk. Locals and visitors work side by side, but Balinese communities lead. Respect the banjar and local customs at every cleanup.

communities.notes: About 3,000 followers and volunteers, founded by two Balinese sisters with an expat-heavy volunteer base. Tension over expats and tourists taking over the visible roles while locals do the community work.

communities.name: Retro Handheld Mods

description.purpose: Backlights, shells, batteries, audio mods: bring your old handhelds back to life.
description.culture: Read the FAQ. No ROM links.

communities.notes: About 15,000 members and a strict FAQ culture. A handful of expert modders answer most technical questions; sellers of mod kits have a lot of informal sway.

communities.name: Gnomon Linux

description.purpose: Gnomon is a minimal, independent Linux distribution built around musl, runit and a ports-style package system. It targets x86_64, aarch64 and riscv64, with reproducible builds and a rolling release model. The base system installs in under 200 MB. Package recipes are plain shell scripts; see the handbook for the build system and the ports tree layout.

communities.notes: About 60 contributors, but in practice the original author holds the signing keys, merges nearly everything, and has the final word in any dispute. None of that is in the description, which is entirely technical.

communities.name: Beit Shalom Havurah

description.purpose:
Beit Shalom is a small, egalitarian, lay-led Jewish community in Buenos Aires. We've been meeting since 2008, first in members' living rooms in Palermo and Villa Crespo, and since 2020 also on Zoom, which brought in members from Córdoba, Rosario and abroad. We're about 60 households.

What we do: Kabbalat Shabbat once a month in person and once on Zoom; High Holiday services; a Torah study group on Tuesday evenings; Passover seder and Purim together; and we support each other through births, b'nei mitzvah, illness and mourning.

We have no rabbi. Services are led by members, who take turns. Anyone who wants to learn to lead can get help from our liturgy group. Divrei Torah are given by whoever volunteers that week. For life-cycle events, families can choose to bring in a rabbi they know.

How we organise ourselves: decisions are made at our general meeting twice a year, where every member household has a vote. Between meetings, a coordinating committee of five volunteers, elected for two years, keeps things running: the calendar, finances, the email list and our relationship with the space we rent for the High Holidays. Members pay what they can; there is no fixed fee.

The current discussion: since the pandemic we've grown, and some members feel that lay leadership is stretching thin. Several families want to hire a part-time rabbi, someone who could teach, support people in crisis and bring more depth to our practice. Others feel that having no rabbi is part of who we are, and worry that a rabbi would end up holding the authority we've always shared. The coordinating committee has prepared a document with both options and the costs, and we'll discuss it at the general meeting in Elul.
description.culture: Warm, questioning and egalitarian. We welcome interfaith families, LGBTQ+ Jews, people who are just curious, and people who aren't sure what they believe. Argue like it's a Talmud page: passionately, respectfully, and with food afterward.

communities.notes: Deliberately non-hierarchical, but a few founding members who lead most services hold a lot of quiet authority. The rabbi debate is really about whether growth means professionalising.

communities.name: Computational Linguistics Reading Group

description.purpose: Weekly reading group for students and researchers in two computational linguistics and NLP labs in Seoul, plus anyone else interested. Every Thursday someone presents a paper (sign up on the spreadsheet), and we discuss it in person and on Discord. We focus on Korean and low-resource language processing, but anything interesting goes.
description.culture: No question is too basic. Presenters don't need to understand everything; just tell us what confused you. Undergrads especially welcome.

communities.notes: About 45 on Discord, 10–15 at each meeting. Started by PhD students in two different labs to get around a frosty relationship between their professors, who never attend.

communities.name: Hedgehog Census

description.purpose: Seen a hedgehog? Tell us where and when.

communities.notes: Run by a wildlife charity with university partners, with an expert team validating records and a big volunteer base of gardeners who mostly never interact with each other. The description says nothing about how data is used or who's behind it.
communities.setupNotes: reporting website; no format fits well

communities.name: Fogata

description.purpose: Fogata ('campfire') is the meeting point for Spanish speakers from all over Latin America and beyond. Chat, game, study, share music, memes and your country's food. Channels for each country, voice rooms that never sleep, and weekly events: movie nights, trivia, karaoke and tournaments.
description.culture: Here it doesn't matter where you're from or how you say 'popcorn'. Zero tolerance for racism, xenophobia and harassment. No NSFW. Respect the staff; if you disagree with a decision, open a ticket.

communities.notes: About 40,000 members, mostly 16–25. Run by an owner and a large staff with ranks and a weekly staff meeting. Mexican and Argentine members dominate, and smaller countries' channels feel like afterthoughts.

communities.name: Dementia Caregivers Kenya

description.purpose:
Dementia Caregivers Kenya is a support network for people caring for a parent, spouse or relative living with dementia. Many of us didn't even know the word 'dementia' until our loved one was diagnosed, or until we realised what was happening. We know how lonely and exhausting caregiving can be, especially when family and neighbours don't understand, and when people say it's just old age, or worse, witchcraft.

We started in 2019 as one WhatsApp group of eight caregivers who met at a hospital talk in Nairobi. Now we have regional groups for Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru and the diaspora, with about 700 members in total, and an in-person meetup in Nairobi on the first Saturday of the month.

What we share:
- Practical tips: bathing, eating, wandering, sleep problems, aggression
- Information about diagnosis, medication and doctors who understand dementia
- How to talk to family and the community
- Support for the caregiver: you matter too

Group rules:
1. Respect and confidentiality. What is shared here stays here.
2. No medical prescriptions. Share your experience, but always consult a doctor about medication.
3. No selling or promoting products, herbs or 'cures'. There is no cure for dementia yet. Anyone promoting one will be removed.
4. No religious debates. Prayers and blessings are welcome, but don't tell anyone their faith is wrong.
5. Kindly post in English or Kiswahili.

Our team: each regional group has two volunteer admins, who are themselves caregivers or former caregivers. The founders, Mama Wanjiru and Dr Otieno, coordinate the network and the meetups.

The recent problem: over the last few months, several people joined the groups to sell supplements and 'brain tonics', some claiming to be caregivers themselves. Some members bought products and lost money. We have removed these people and now admins speak to every new member by phone before adding them. This has slowed down joining, and we're sorry if you've had to wait.
description.culture: Pole sana, you're not alone. We listen without judging, we laugh when we can, and we hold each other up.

communities.notes: Mostly daughters and wives caring for elderly relatives, plus some diaspora children managing care remotely. The phone-screening fix works but depends on a few overstretched admins, and the founders' views carry great weight.

communities.name: Le Chantier Collectif

description.purpose: We're an architecture and construction collective in Marseille working on social housing renovation, reuse of building materials, and participatory design with residents. Mattermost is our shared workspace: projects, the materials bank, finances, and the Thursday collective meeting.
description.culture: We started as five friends around a table and decided everything together over lunch. We're thirty now, and we're still trying to work that way, but honestly we're figuring it out. New people: ask anyone anything, and come to Thursdays even if you don't understand everything yet. We're writing down how we make decisions; the draft is in #how-we-work.

communities.notes: Grew from 5 to 30 in about a year after winning two big public contracts. The founders still decide most things informally over lunch, often without realising it, and newer members feel excluded from a 'flat' structure that has an obvious inner circle.

communities.name: Harbour Town Bowls Club

description.purpose: Lawn bowls on the Harbour Town greens. Social bowls Wednesday and Saturday, pennants in season, barefoot bowls for groups.

communities.notes: About 120 members on the Facebook page, mostly retirees. Run by a traditional elected committee, which is quietly worried about whether the club will survive another decade.

communities.name: Yoruba Language Hangout

description.purpose: A Discord for anyone learning or speaking Yoruba: heritage speakers who understand but can't reply, total beginners, and fluent speakers who want to help. We have voice practice rooms, a word of the day, channels for proverbs, music and Nollywood, and weekly beginner sessions on Sunday.
description.culture: Don't laugh at anyone's tones; we're all learning. Fluent speakers, be patient. All dialects welcome. If you correct someone, explain why.

communities.notes: About 900 members, mostly diaspora young adults in the UK and US, plus a few volunteer tutors in Nigeria. Two founders run it; there's mild tension over whether Standard Yoruba or regional dialects should be taught.

communities.name: Lanternfish Comic Patrons

description.purpose:
Hey, I'm Sol, and I draw Lanternfish, a webcomic about a lighthouse keeper's daughter who finds a city under the sea. This is the Patreon and Discord for the people who keep it going.

Here's the unusual part. Since chapter 4, patrons have helped decide where the story goes. At the end of each chapter, I post two or three possible directions (sometimes four if I can't choose). Patrons vote over a week, and the winning direction becomes the next chapter. I still write and draw everything, and I decide how we get there, but you decide where we go.

How voting works:
- Every patron gets one vote per chapter, regardless of tier. I did this on purpose; I don't want the story to belong to whoever pays the most.
- Voting is in the #story-votes channel, with a poll and a discussion thread. Arguments for your choice are encouraged. Some of the best ideas came from those threads.
- I can veto an option before it goes to vote (if it doesn't fit the world, or I just can't draw it), but once it's up, the vote is binding. I've never overturned one, even when I really wanted to (RIP Captain Mareth).

Other things in the Discord: #process for sketches and thumbnails, #fan-art, #theories, and #off-topic. Higher tiers get page previews and monthly drawing streams.

Rules:
1. Be kind, especially in vote threads. It's a comic, not an election.
2. Spoilers for unreleased pages stay in patron channels.
3. Fan art is welcome and you keep the rights to it; don't sell my characters, though.

My partner Jae and two longtime patrons, Mo and Kit, moderate.

The current situation: chapter 9's vote was the closest ever, and the winning option (by 11 votes) was the 'dark' path, which a lot of people really didn't want. Some patrons have asked for ranked-choice voting, others for a minimum turnout, and a few have suggested I just take back control of the story. I'm thinking about it, and would love to hear what you think in #meta.
description.culture: Cosy, imaginative, and occasionally very intense about fictional sea creatures.

communities.notes: About 2,500 patrons. Sol gives patrons real narrative power, which is rare and why many people join, but it means creator-community dynamics are tangled up with something like a small democracy, complete with factions.

communities.name: MetaMuseum DAO

description.purpose: MetaMuseum is a community-run virtual museum of digital art. Members propose and vote on exhibitions, acquisitions and artist grants, and every season we elect three curators who put together the shows. Hang out in Discord, join gallery walk-throughs, and submit your work to open calls.
description.culture: Art first, price second. Critique is welcome, shilling is not. Curators are accountable to members and give a public report every season.

communities.notes: About 3,000 Discord members, a few hundred token holders who vote. Curator elections are lively but turnout is low, and wealthy collectors' votes count for more than artists'.

communities.name: Dmitri's Chess Lab

description.purpose: My server. Lessons, puzzles, game analysis, and me yelling about bad openings.

communities.notes: A Tbilisi chess coach's personal server, about 50 people. Paying students get lesson channels and the rest are friends and fans; Dmitri rules absolutely, but students expect something closer to a class with fair treatment.

communities.name: Haddad Family Reunion

description.purpose: Planning the big Haddad reunion in Zahle next summer! This is where we collect dates, flights, who's staying where, and ideas for the program. We have family coming from Lebanon, France, Canada, Brazil and Australia. Fill in the spreadsheet so we know numbers.
description.culture: Everyone's opinion is welcome, but Tante Mona and Rania are making final decisions, otherwise we will never agree on anything 😅. French, English, Arabic, Portuguese: we'll manage!

communities.notes: About 60 relatives on WhatsApp plus an email thread for older ones. Two organisers decide, but the Brazil and Australia branches feel their dates were ignored, and old family feuds keep surfacing in the planning.

communities.name: Saturday Five-a-Side

description.purpose:
Saturday morning football, 7am, at the pitch in Lekki Phase 1. Four teams of five plus subs, winner stays on. This group is for confirming who's playing, pitch fees, and banter.

How it works:
- By Thursday 8pm, reply with your name on the list Chidi posts. First 22 names play. After that you're on the reserve list.
- Pitch fee is N5,000 per head per week, paid to Chidi before kick-off or by transfer. No pay, no play. We've been carrying too many people.
- Teams are picked on the morning by the two captains of the week. Captains rotate alphabetically so no one moans about favouritism.
- If you put your name down and don't show without telling us by Friday night, you still pay. Two no-shows in a month and you go to the bottom of the list for the next month.
- Bibs: whoever took them home brings them back washed.

The ongoing wahala: some people owe for weeks, one guy owes almost two months. Chidi has been covering the shortfall to keep the pitch booking, which isn't fair to him. We agreed that from next month, anyone owing more than two weeks can't play until they clear it, and debts will be posted in the group. Some think posting names is too harsh; we'll see if it works.
description.culture: Play hard, no dangerous tackles, no fighting. Banter is fine, but leave people's mothers out of it. What happens on the pitch stays on the pitch.

communities.notes: 22 regulars plus reserves, mostly young professionals. Chidi has no official role but controls the list, the money and the booking, so he's the de facto chairman, and the debt-shaming plan has divided the group.

communities.name: Kallio Block Party Committee

description.purpose: We organise the yearly Kallio block party on our street, plus the flea market in spring and the Christmas courtyard evening. This Telegram group is for planning: permits, music, food stalls, volunteers, and cleanup.
description.culture: Mikko started this in 2017 and basically ran it until he moved to Tampere in the autumn (thanks for everything, Mikko!). Now it's up to all of us. We're figuring out who does what. Please volunteer for something on the list, even if it's small. Nobody is in charge yet, so speak up if you want to help coordinate.

communities.notes: About 90 neighbours. Mikko held all the contacts (the city permit office, the sound guy, the café) and did everything himself. Nobody has stepped up to replace him, and two people quietly competing for the role are making things awkward.

communities.name: Open Council Mombasa

description.purpose: Live updates from Mombasa County Assembly sittings, so you know what your MCAs are deciding.

communities.notes: Run by three volunteer journalists and a civic-tech NGO. The X replies are a free-for-all, while the website posts are edited carefully to avoid defamation.

communities.name: Carvalho & Reis Architects

description.purpose: Internal Teams workspace for Carvalho & Reis Architects. Each project has its own channel with drawings, client notes and deadlines. The General channel is for studio news, the Studio Ops channel for IT, supplies and room bookings. The Friday design review is in the big room and online.
description.culture: Clear, punctual and courteous. Raise problems early. The partners have an open door; please use it.

communities.notes: About 28 staff: two partners, associates, architects and interns. The partners make all major decisions, and interns are often overworked before deadlines, which the 'open door' doesn't really address.

communities.name: Midwives' Exchange

description.purpose:
Midwives' Exchange is a professional discussion forum for qualified midwives and student midwives worldwide. It began in 2003 as an email list run by a group of independent midwives in the UK and Australia, moved to a web forum in 2011, and to its current Discourse platform in 2021. We now have about 4,000 members in more than 60 countries.

What we discuss: clinical practice and evidence, cases (anonymised), home birth and birth centres, midwifery education, regulation and professional issues, and the emotional side of the work.

Who can join: qualified midwives, student midwives and midwifery academics. Doulas, obstetricians and other professionals can join as associate members with access to most categories.

Rules:
1. Patient confidentiality is absolute. Remove all identifying details, including dates and locations, before discussing a case.
2. Back clinical claims with evidence or say clearly that it's your experience.
3. Respect different models of care and practice settings. A midwife in a rural clinic in Malawi and one in a London teaching hospital face different realities.
4. No product promotion.
5. Debate ideas, not people.

The forum is run by an elected council of seven volunteers, who appoint category moderators.

What's going on: since the move to Discourse, many younger midwives have joined, often bringing a more informal style, more posts about burnout and workplace bullying, and humour that some longtime members find unprofessional. At the same time, some newer members feel the 'old guard' dismisses their experiences and polices tone more than content. A heated thread about whether memes should be allowed led to several resignations from both sides. The council has set up a working group, with members from both groups, to review our guidelines and propose changes at the next annual members' meeting.
description.culture: Professional, evidence-based, and supportive. We take the work seriously, and we look after each other, because nobody else understands it quite like another midwife.

communities.notes: A long-established professional community going through a generational shift. The fight over tone is a proxy for who the forum is for: senior independent midwives or a broader, younger workforce dealing with burnout.

communities.name: Calculus II Study Group

description.purpose: Study group for students taking Calculus II this semester at the university. We share notes, solutions to exercises after the deadline, past exam papers, and explain things to each other. Online study sessions on Zalo video every Tuesday and Friday evening before exams.
description.culture: Help each other, no copying before deadlines. Explaining a problem helps you learn it too. Don't be shy about asking basic questions; half the class is confused anyway.

communities.notes: About 60 students organised by two class monitors, no teacher involved. The rule about not sharing solutions before deadlines is often broken, and the monitors are unsure whether to enforce it.

communities.name: Four-Day Week Now

description.purpose: Weekly newsletter for the campaign to make a 32-hour, four-day week normal, with no loss of pay.

communities.notes: About 20,000 subscribers, run by a small paid team at a think tank. Supporters can't talk to each other at all; the 'movement' is a broadcast list plus occasional petitions.

communities.name: Online Chadō Practice

description.purpose: Online study group for students of the Way of Tea, under the guidance of our teacher. We gather on Zoom twice a month to practise temae together and to study the seasons, utensils and history of tea. In the LINE group, the teacher shares announcements and senior students answer questions.
description.culture: We follow the traditional etiquette of the tea room, even online. Please address the teacher as Sensei. Questions about practice go first to your senior (sempai), who will bring them to Sensei if needed. Please do not share recordings or post photos of lessons on social media. Gratitude and humility in all things.

communities.notes: About 50 students in Japan and abroad. A hobby group, but run with strict teacher authority and a seniority hierarchy; new students sometimes find it intimidating, and asking Sensei directly is a serious breach of etiquette.

communities.name: OpenGauge

description.purpose:
OpenGauge is an open dataset of river and stream levels collected from public gauging stations around the world, cleaned up and published in a single consistent format, along with tools to download and work with the data. It's used by hydrologists, flood forecasters, kayakers, farmers and journalists. Code and data live on GitHub; discussion happens on our Discourse.

We started in 2020 because one of us got fed up with scraping 40 different national websites in 40 different formats. Today we cover about 18,000 stations in 60 countries, updated daily.

How to contribute:
- Add a new data source: write a scraper following the template in /sources, with tests. One maintainer reviews it.
- Fix data: if you spot bad readings, open an issue with the station ID, date range and what's wrong. Don't 'correct' data silently; we flag suspect values rather than delete them.
- Improve tools, docs or translations.

Data quality rules:
- We never alter raw values. Cleaning and quality flags are added as separate columns.
- Every station has a clear source attribution and licence.
- Sources that don't allow redistribution are not included, even if the data is technically public.

Governance: there are five maintainers with merge rights. Decisions are made by lazy consensus in public issues: if nobody objects within a week, it goes ahead. Bigger decisions (new licence, new maintainers) need agreement from at least four of the five. New maintainers are invited after sustained contributions.

The current debate: a big commercial weather company wants to fund the project, which would pay for servers and a part-time maintainer. They'd like early access to new data sources. Our data is CC-BY, so they could use it anyway, but early access would mean holding back new sources from the public for a few weeks. Some maintainers think it's a reasonable trade for sustainability; others think it breaks what OpenGauge is for. The discussion is in the 'Funding proposal' thread, and we welcome input from users, especially those in countries whose data we use.
description.culture: Careful, open and practical. Thank people for bug reports. Assume the person who wrote the scraper you're fixing did their best with a terrible government website.

communities.notes: About 200 contributors with five maintainers doing most of the work for free. The funding debate is about sustainability versus openness, and users in data-source countries (often the Global South) have little voice in the maintainers' decision.

communities.name: Temple Youth Seva

description.purpose: Discord for the youth volunteers (seva) at the temple, ages 14–25. Sign up for seva shifts at festivals and weekly events, coordinate Diwali, Navratri and Holi prep, share bhajan practice recordings, and hang out. Service hours are tracked for school volunteering requirements.
description.culture: Seva is service without expecting anything back, but snacks are provided. Be respectful in temple channels. Youth coordinators are here to help; the temple board approves events.

communities.notes: About 150 young people, run by three young adult coordinators supervised by a temple board member. Teens love the Discord; parents and the board get uneasy about what goes on in the off-topic channels.

communities.name: Mbatha Paleoclimate Lab

description.purpose: Reconstructing southern African rainfall over the last 200,000 years from cave speleothems and lake sediments.

communities.notes: A lab of about 12 people at a Cape Town university, with a PI, a lab manager and students; much of their governance is about fieldwork permits and sharing expensive instrument time. The description only covers the science.

communities.name: Céu Escuro Brasil

description.purpose: Volunteers measuring light pollution across Brazil. With a cheap sky quality meter or just your eyes and our star charts, you can record how dark your sky is and add it to the national map. In the Telegram group we share how to measure, compare results, and plan measurement nights during new moons.
description.culture: Anyone can join, from the middle of São Paulo to the backlands. Measure honestly, even if your sky is terrible; that's data too. Respect the method so we can trust the results.

communities.notes: About 350 volunteers, coordinated by an astronomer at a federal university and a few amateur astronomy club leaders. Data quality checks are done by the coordinator alone, which creates a backlog.

communities.name: Agora Hellas

description.purpose:
Agora Hellas has been the largest Greek-language discussion forum since 2003. Whether you're in Athens, Thessaloniki, a village in Crete, or Melbourne, this is a place to talk about everything: news, technology, cars, cooking, football, travel, jobs, and anything else on your mind. We have about 70,000 registered members and thousands of posts every day.

Main sections: News & Society, Politics, Technology, Sports, Life & Relationships, Economy & Work, Diaspora, Marketplace, and Off-topic.

History of moderation: in the first years, the forum had very few rules, and the politics section became so toxic that many members left. After the 2011–2012 crisis years, when debates about the memoranda, the elections and migration turned into personal attacks and threats, the administration introduced the current rules and expanded the moderation team. In 2020 the politics section was split into a moderated 'Political Debate' section and a closed archive.

Current rules:
1. No personal attacks, threats or doxxing. Criticise ideas, not members.
2. In Political Debate, every claim of fact must be supported with a source if challenged. Insulting groups of people based on their nationality, religion or origin is forbidden.
3. No fake news. Posts that spread proven false information will be marked or removed.
4. One account per person. Duplicate accounts are banned.
5. No advertising outside the Marketplace.
6. Moderators' decisions can be appealed to the administration through private message, not in public threads.

The forum is privately owned. The administration (the owner and two admins) sets policy, and about 20 volunteer moderators enforce it section by section.

Today's challenge: Agora is getting older. Younger Greeks are on social media and Discord, and our active membership is shrinking every year. Some members want the forum to modernise; others say its value is exactly that it's slow and text-based. The administration is consulting with members about the future in the 'Agora 2030' thread.
description.culture: A place for real discussion, the way Greeks like it: passionate and loud, but with respect.

communities.notes: A privately owned forum with a large, ageing user base and a strong moderation tradition born of past toxicity. The owner holds ultimate power; 'consulting' members is new and nobody is sure how much it means.

communities.name: Fluent Enough

description.purpose: A Discord for people who stammer or stutter, of all ages and from all over. We have voice rooms for low-pressure speaking practice, channels for job interviews and phone anxiety, speech therapy experiences (good and bad), and just chatting with people who get it.
description.culture: Take all the time you need. Never finish someone's sentence. No 'have you tried slowing down?'. Stammer proudly or work on fluency; both are valid here.

communities.notes: About 1,100 members, mostly teens and young adults. Run by four volunteer mods who stammer. There's a quiet split between people who embrace stammering as identity and those seeking fluency therapy.

communities.name: Cooperativa de Taxis del Cerro

description.purpose: Group for members of the taxi cooperative: shifts, assemblies, notices.

communities.notes: About 300 driver-owners in Montevideo with an elected board and monthly assemblies. Competition from ride apps has made assemblies tense; older and younger drivers disagree about joining a platform.

communities.name: Kraków Astronomy Society

description.purpose: The Kraków branch of the national amateur astronomy society. Members meet for monthly lectures at the observatory, organise observing nights outside the city, run public stargazing events, and share equipment. This mailing list is for meeting announcements, observing plans, and equipment questions.
description.culture: We welcome beginners as much as experienced observers. Please keep discussions on astronomy. Members borrowing society telescopes are responsible for returning them in good condition.

communities.notes: About 220 members, run by a branch board elected every three years. Mostly older men; the board would like younger members but is suspicious of moving to Discord, where the younger members already are.

communities.name: Euskal Etxea Berria

description.purpose:
Euskal Etxea Berria ('New Basque House') is a Basque cultural association in Boise for anyone who wants to keep the Basque language and culture alive in Idaho and the Intermountain West: dancing, music, pelota, cooking, and above all, Euskara, the Basque language.

We were founded this spring by members who left the older Basque club in town. We don't want to be enemies; many of us still have family and friends there, and we'll keep showing up at the big community events. But we split because we disagreed about the future, and especially about the language.

What we believe: Euskara is the heart of Basque identity, and it's disappearing here. The older club's activities happen almost entirely in English, and Euskara classes have been an afterthought. We want a place where the language comes first: where events start with Euskara, where kids can learn it, and where people who don't speak it yet are welcomed and supported to learn.

What we're doing:
- Weekly Euskara classes for adults (beginner and intermediate) and a Saturday morning language play group for kids
- A monthly mintzapraktika (conversation evening) at a bar downtown
- Dance practice for kids and adults
- Collaborating with the Basque Government's diaspora programs

How we're organised: we're registering as a nonprofit. Right now we have a founding board of five, elected at our first general meeting in April, which will serve until next year's elections. Membership is open to anyone, Basque or not, who supports our mission, for $40 per family per year. All members can vote at general meetings.

On our Facebook group and email list: please be respectful toward the other club and its members, even when you disagree. No gossip about who went where. We want to be judged by what we build, not by what we left.
description.culture: Ongi etorri, welcome. We're serious about the language but not snobbish: every word you learn counts. Family-friendly, warm, and a little bit stubborn, like Basques are.

communities.notes: About 400 people on Facebook and email. A new group defined partly by its split from a much older club; many families have members in both, and the 'no gossip' rule is hard to keep in a small community.

communities.name: Cozy Hollow

description.purpose: Welcome to the Hollow! This is the community for Bramble, your sleepy forest-spirit VTuber. Hang out between streams, share fanart, join community game nights, and get notified when Bramble goes live (usually Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday evenings, EU time).
description.culture: Cozy vibes only. No backseating during streams, no asking about Bramble's real identity, no lewd fanart. Mods' decisions are final. Be a good Hollowling 🍄

communities.notes: About 8,000 Discord members, with mods drawn from top supporters. Bramble sets the tone but rarely moderates; the 'no identity' rule is strictly enforced and is the main reason people get banned.

communities.name: SeedVault DAO

description.purpose: Funding community seed banks that protect heirloom and indigenous crop varieties. Stake, propose, vote.

communities.notes: About 500 members, mostly crypto-native donors in Europe and North America; the seed banks themselves, in Ethiopia, Peru and India, have no votes. Proposals are written by the founding team.

communities.name: Amara's Voice Notes

description.purpose: Every morning I record a short voice note: what I'm thinking about, what I'm grateful for, something I read, sometimes just me ranting about traffic in Accra. It started for my sisters and a few friends; now there are a few hundred of you. You can react, and I read every reply that comes to my DMs.
description.culture: This is a soft place. Listen when you can, skip when you can't. If you forward a note, forward the whole thing, not a clip without context.

communities.notes: A WhatsApp channel with about 200 followers, so only Amara can post. Feels intimate and personal, but she's started getting brand offers and isn't sure whether accepting would ruin it.

communities.name: The Ramírez-Okoro Household

description.purpose:
This is our family chat and calendar for the seven of us: Dani and Chidi, plus Sofía (16), Mateo (13), Ada (11), Kelechi (9), and baby Ngozi, and occasionally Grandma when she visits.

What goes where:
- The shared calendar has everyone's schedule, including which weekends Sofía and Mateo are at their dad's and which weeks Ada and Kelechi are with their mom. Check it before making plans. If it's not on the calendar, it doesn't exist.
- The chat is for pickups, 'who took my charger', dinner votes, and memes.

House agreements (made at the family meeting in January, signed by everyone, on the fridge):
- Chores rotate weekly. The chart is pinned. If you trade a chore, both of you have to say so in the chat.
- Screens off at 9pm on school nights for the younger three, 10pm for Sofía and Mateo. Phones charge in the kitchen overnight. Parents too (we're trying).
- Sunday dinner is mandatory for whoever's home. Everyone takes a turn picking the meal.
- Family meeting first Sunday of the month. Anyone can add to the agenda in the chat. Kids get a vote on things that affect everyone, like holidays and chores. Parents have the final say on safety and money.
- No one goes in anyone else's room without knocking. This applies to Kelechi.

What's hard: Sofía and Mateo feel the rules are stricter here than at their dad's, and Ada says the chore chart favours the older kids because they're away every other weekend. We're going to talk about both at the next family meeting.
description.culture: We're still learning how to be one family. Be patient, say sorry, and assume good intentions. Mateo, stop renaming the chat.

communities.notes: A blended family of seven in Houston with two custody schedules. The parents use quite formal structures (meetings, votes, signed agreements) to keep things fair, but the older kids see them as house rules imposed by a step-parent.

communities.name: The Hike Crew

description.purpose: We started as a few friends hiking Doi Suthep on weekends. Now people keep inviting their friends and friends of friends, and we're about 60! Hikes are posted here on Wednesday for the weekend: trail, meeting point, difficulty, and who's leading.
description.culture: Friendly and chill. Hike at your own pace, nobody gets left behind, and take your trash with you. Since we're getting bigger, please don't add people without asking Nok or Ben first, and bring water, seriously.

communities.notes: Expats and Thais mixed, with Nok and Ben (the original pair) still informally in charge. They're now dealing with safety questions, people they've never met showing up, and whether to set up rules or even liability waivers, none of which fits a friend group.
communities.setupNotes: could be hobby now that it's growing

communities.name: Rua Augusta 112 Residents

description.purpose: Residents of Rua Augusta 112: building notices, deliveries, maintenance.

communities.notes: About 40 residents of a São Paulo building, with the building manager (síndica) as admin. The chat carries notices but real decisions happen at the formal condominium assembly, which few attend.

communities.name: Library Futures Aarhus

description.purpose: Aarhus Municipality wants to hear from you about the future of our local libraries. Should branches be open without staff in the evenings? Should they offer more workshops, quiet study spaces, or citizen services? Share your ideas, comment on others' suggestions, and vote on proposals. Input will be summarised for the city council in the spring.
description.culture: All residents are welcome, including children and young people. Keep it constructive and on topic. A moderator from the library service reads all posts and answers questions weekly.

communities.notes: About 600 participants, mostly older regular library users and parents. Staff unions are worried that 'staff-free hours' is a cost-cutting plan and are posting a lot, which makes the library-service moderator's position awkward.

communities.name: Willowmere Care Staff

description.purpose:
This group started as a way for care staff at Willowmere House to swap shifts and cover each other. It still is. Post swaps here, and let the shift lead know.

But over the past year it's become more than that. After the changes to night shift staffing in the spring, when the company cut nights from four carers to three without asking anyone, a lot of us realised we needed to talk to each other, and to management, as a group. So now this is also where we:
- Share what's happening on different floors and shifts, so nobody's on their own with a problem
- Collect concerns about staffing, safety and pay to raise together
- Plan what to say at staff meetings, and who will say it
- Support people who are having a hard time with a manager

We are not officially a union. About a third of us are members of a union, and a rep has visited a couple of times, but most people aren't, and some are worried about joining. That's fine. You don't have to be a union member to be in this group.

Our agreements:
- Nothing about residents goes in this chat. Ever. No names, no rooms, no details. If something about care worries you, report it properly.
- What's said here stays here. Don't screenshot to management.
- Nobody speaks for everyone without asking first. If you're raising something with management as 'the staff', check here.
- Be kind about each other. We all work hard.

Recently, management asked to join the group 'to improve communication'. We said no, politely. We think they may set up their own official group, and we'll keep this one for us.
description.culture: We look after the residents, and we look after each other. Nobody gets left on their own.

communities.notes: About 45 carers, kitchen and cleaning staff, many of them migrant workers. It's both a practical workplace group and an informal union, and the people quietly leading the organising are taking a risk with their jobs.

communities.name: Product Designers Bangladesh

description.purpose: Community for product, UX and UI designers in Bangladesh. Share your work for feedback, find jobs and freelance gigs, learn about tools and case studies, and meet at our monthly Dhaka meetups. Discord for chat and portfolio reviews; the Facebook group for job posts and announcements.
description.culture: Help juniors grow. Feedback should be specific and kind. No piracy links for design tools. Job posts must include salary range.

communities.notes: About 3,500 members, run by a few senior designers from big local tech companies. The salary-range rule is popular with juniors and often ignored by employers, and admins disagree on how strictly to enforce it.

communities.name: French 2, Period 4

description.purpose: Assignments, vocab lists and announcements for Madame Dubois's French 2, period 4.

communities.notes: 28 sophomores at a US public high school. Only the teacher posts; students can comment privately to her. The class's social life happens elsewhere.

communities.name: Bring Back the Tram

description.purpose: Ljubljana's tram was removed in 1958. We want it back. Our demands: a modern tram line from Bežigrad to the centre and on to Vič within ten years; a dedicated lane on Slovenska and Dunajska; full integration with buses under one ticket; and a public feasibility study commissioned before the next municipal budget. Cities of similar size across Europe have shown that trams reduce car traffic, emissions and noise.

communities.notes: About 2,000 supporters, organised by a handful of urbanism students and a retired transport engineer, who make decisions over coffee. The description is pure policy; it says nothing about who decides or how anyone can get involved.

communities.name: The Velvet Spool

description.purpose:
The Velvet Spool is a fan community for Marrowdeep, the gothic period drama that ran for six seasons and broke our hearts. We've been here since season one (2014). The forum is for meta, episode rewatches, fan theories and creative discussion, and our archive collection hosts more than 9,000 fanworks.

What's here:
- Forum: Episode discussion, character meta, rewatch threads, fanfic recommendations, fan art, cosplay, and the general off-topic 'Parlour'.
- Archive collection: we host fic and art for Marrowdeep, organised by our tagging guidelines. Moderated: works are checked for correct tags before they appear.
- Events: the annual Midwinter Exchange (secret gift fic and art), Rarepair Week, and the season rewatch every autumn.

Rules:
1. Tag your work. Ratings, warnings and pairings must follow the tagging guide. This is how people find what they want and avoid what they don't. Mis-tagged works are hidden until fixed.
2. Don't yuck someone's yum. You don't have to like every pairing. You do have to leave people who like it alone. No hate in comments, no posting someone's fic elsewhere to mock it.
3. Fiction is fiction. Content that's legal and properly tagged is allowed. Real-person fic about the actors is not.
4. No harassing cast, crew or writers, including the showrunner who wrote the finale (yes, we know).

The forum is run by four mods; the archive by three archivists. Mods are elected by members every two years.

This year: the Gideon/Lucien vs Gideon/Clara ship war, which has been simmering since season three, blew up again after a popular writer posted a meta essay that one side called 'shipper propaganda'. Threads were locked, two members were banned for harassment, and some people accused the mods of favouring one side because two of them ship Gideon/Lucien. We've just had mod elections early because of it. The new mod team includes people from both ships and a neutral (bless her). We'd really like everyone to take a breath.
description.culture: Creative, generous and very, very invested. We love Marrowdeep enough to argue about it for ten years.

communities.notes: About 6,000 members, long after the show ended. Elected mods and strict tagging make it orderly, but fannish factions treat moderation decisions as partisan, and every mod election becomes a referendum on the ship war.

communities.name: Kanji Stroke Data

description.purpose: An open dataset of stroke order and stroke shape data for Japanese kanji and kana, as SVG paths with stroke numbering. Used in dictionary apps, flashcards and handwriting recognition. Contributions welcome: fixes, missing characters, regional variants.
description.culture: Please cite your source for any stroke order correction (we follow Ministry of Education guidance, with variants noted separately). Be patient with reviews; we're three people with day jobs.

communities.notes: About 40 contributors, but three maintainers review everything. Debates about variant stroke orders can run for months, and the maintainers' word is final.

communities.name: Online Quaker Meeting

description.purpose: Silent worship online, Sundays 10:30. Business is decided together by the sense of the meeting, with no votes.

communities.notes: About 80 Friends from several countries, with a clerk who discerns 'the sense of the meeting' rather than counting votes. A decision can take months, and newcomers are often baffled at how anything gets decided.

communities.name: Behavioural Ecology Lab

description.purpose: Workspace for the Behavioural Ecology Lab at Lund. We study mate choice, parental care and migration in birds and fish. Teams for formal lab business (meetings, documents, safety), Slack for day-to-day chat, field season planning and R help.
description.culture: Ask for help with stats before it's too late. Field season is intense, so look after each other. Lab meeting on Wednesdays; everyone presents in turn.

communities.notes: About 22 people with two co-PIs who disagree on many things, so students sometimes get conflicting guidance. Using both Teams and Slack is a running joke and a real source of missed messages.

communities.name: Butterfly Volunteers of Catalonia

description.purpose:
We're the network of volunteers who walk butterfly transects across Catalonia, Andorra and the Balearic Islands. Each volunteer walks a fixed route, usually one to three kilometres, once a week from March to September, and records every butterfly seen within a set distance. The data goes into a long-term monitoring program that has been running since 1994, and is used to track the effects of climate change, land abandonment and agriculture on butterfly populations across Europe.

Who can join: anyone who can commit to walking a route regularly and learning to identify butterflies. You don't need to be an expert to start. We'll pair you with an experienced volunteer for your first season.

How it works:
- New volunteers attend a training day in spring (identification, the method, using the app).
- You choose an existing route that needs someone or propose a new one, which the coordination team will review for suitability.
- You walk the route each week in suitable weather (sunny or partly cloudy, little wind, warm enough) and enter counts in the app.
- Difficult identifications: take a photo and post it to the identification channel, or mark the record as 'uncertain' and an expert will check it.
- At the end of the season, data is validated by the coordinators before being added to the database.

The program is run by a small coordination team at a natural history museum, with regional coordinators who are themselves experienced volunteers.

On the mailing list: share sightings, ask questions, and announce field trips. Please don't share exact locations of rare species publicly; send them to the coordinators.

This year's issue: several long-term volunteers, who have walked their routes for more than 20 years, are retiring, and we're struggling to find new volunteers for routes in rural areas. If you know anyone, please let us know.
description.culture: Patient, precise, and happy to spend a morning watching a meadow. Long-standing volunteers are generous with their knowledge.

communities.notes: About 500 volunteers, many retired, with a strong method and expert validation. The real risk is not conflict but succession: routes with decades of data could go dark.

communities.name: Tiled

description.purpose: Tiled is a new kind of social network: post photos, thoughts and links as tiles, arrange them into boards, and follow people and boards you like. No algorithmic feed, no ads. We're in public beta and growing fast. Thank you, all 30,000 of you!
description.culture: We're building this with you. Our community guidelines are a work in progress (version 0.4 is on the help page), and we're hiring moderators. In the meantime, use the report button and be patient with us. Feedback goes in the #beta-feedback board.

communities.notes: Owned by a small startup with VC funding. It went from 2,000 to 30,000 users in two months, with a tiny trust and safety team, so the rules are being written while harassment and spam incidents are already happening.

communities.name: Endo Warriors Nigeria

description.purpose: Support for women living with endometriosis in Nigeria: doctors who listen, pain tips, and each other.
description.culture: We believe you.

communities.notes: About 1,500 members across several WhatsApp groups, founded by a woman who was misdiagnosed for years. Recommendations of specific doctors and herbal remedies cause friction, and the admins have no medical training.

communities.name: Fairground Grocery Co-op

description.purpose: News and member updates from Fairground Grocery, the community-owned grocery store in the Longfellow neighborhood. Anyone can shop; members own a share, vote in board elections, and get patronage refunds when we have a good year. This email list is for member news, board meeting notices, and calls for input.
description.culture: Good food, fair prices, local farmers, and a store that belongs to the neighborhood. Board meetings are open to all members. We want to hear from you, especially if you've never come to one.

communities.notes: About 4,000 member-owners, but board elections draw a few hundred votes. The board and the general manager set direction, and a recent push by staff to unionise has made relations with the board tense.

communities.name: Leith Dragon Boat Club

description.purpose:
Leith Dragon Boat Club paddles out of the Water of Leith and the Forth, year-round, in all weathers (within reason). We train twice a week and race in festivals across Scotland, the UK and, every few years, at international events.

We have two crews:
- The Leith Dragons, our open crew, for anyone over 16 who wants to paddle and race.
- The Pink Ladies of Leith, our breast cancer survivors' crew, founded in 2012. Paddling has been shown to help with lymphoedema and recovery after treatment, but for most of us it's about being on the water with women who understand. The Pink Ladies race in breast cancer paddler divisions, and every race ends with a flower ceremony for those we've lost.

The two crews train together on Saturdays and separately on weekdays. The Pink Ladies also meet for coffee after training, and there's a separate private WhatsApp group for support between sessions, open only to survivors.

How the club runs: we're a constituted club with a committee elected at the AGM: chair, secretary, treasurer, head coach, welfare officer, and a representative from each crew. Membership fees cover boat storage, insurance and coaching.

The ongoing discussion: the club has grown and the open crew is more competitive. Some open crew members want more boat time and coaching for racing. Some Pink Ladies feel the club is becoming more about winning, and worry about losing the gentleness that brought them in. At the same time, the Pink Ladies are the reason many of our sponsors and funders support the club. The committee is working on a plan for sharing boats and coaches more fairly, which will go to the AGM.
description.culture: Everyone in the boat pulls together. Competitive but kind. We celebrate every finish line, whatever the time.

communities.notes: About 90 members. Half sports club, half survivors' support group, with different needs that share boats, coaches and a committee, and the Pink Ladies' fundraising power gives them leverage they're uncomfortable using.

communities.name: Filipino Seafarers' Families

description.purpose: For wives, husbands, parents and children of Filipino seafarers. Share news about manning agencies, allotments, contracts and the long months apart. Ask questions about benefits, insurance and what to do when there's a problem on board. And support each other when the ship is far and the loneliness is heavy.
description.culture: We are all one family here. No selling, no loan offers, no gossip about other people's spouses. Respect privacy: don't post vessel names or crew details. Prayers and encouragement always welcome.

communities.notes: About 10,000 members, mostly wives in the Philippines. Admins are seafarers' wives themselves. Agency recruiters and loan sharks constantly try to get in, and gossip about infidelity is the hardest thing to moderate.

communities.name: Late Bus

description.purpose: A weekly essay written on the last bus home. Reply and tell me about yours.

communities.notes: About 900 subscribers. The comments are a small, kind community the writer reads but doesn't moderate; nothing has ever gone wrong, so nothing is written down.

communities.name: Quorum Café DAO

description.purpose: Quorum is a real café in Lisbon's Arroios neighbourhood, owned by its community through a DAO. Members buy a membership NFT, which gives them a vote on the menu, events, opening hours and how profits are used, plus a discount at the counter. Baristas are employed by a local company that the DAO controls, and also hold memberships.
description.culture: Good coffee, good people, transparent decisions. Proposals are discussed on Discord for a week and voted on in Snapshot. Whether you're a crypto person or just love the croissants, you're welcome.

communities.notes: About 300 members, half in Lisbon and half remote crypto fans who've never visited. It works like a co-op but via tokens, so remote members vote on things like opening hours that only affect local staff and regulars.

communities.name: Yusuf's Bike Repair

description.purpose:
Hi, I'm Yusuf. I fix bikes in a tiny workshop in Kadıköy and write about it. The blog started in 2018 as notes for myself: how to true a wheel, why your gears skip, how to keep an old steel frame alive. Somehow people started reading it, and asking questions in the comments, and then asking for a place to talk to each other. So in 2022 I set up the Discord.

It's about 300 people now, mostly in Istanbul but also elsewhere in Turkey and a few abroad. People post photos of their problems, help each other fix things, swap parts, and plan Sunday rides along the Bosphorus.

How to ask for help:
- Post in #help with photos, the bike type, and what you've tried already.
- Be patient. I'm one person with a workshop to run. Other members often answer faster than me, and many of them know as much as I do.
- Don't DM me for free repair advice. Post in #help so everyone can learn.

Other rules:
- Parts swaps are welcome in #market. Selling stolen bikes or parts gets you banned and reported, no discussion.
- No arguing about which brand is best. Ride what you have.
- Advertising your own shop: ask me first.

I'm the only admin. Two regulars, Elif and Kerem, help me moderate.

Honestly, I'm not sure how big I want this to get. A few people have suggested a membership fee, or classes, or turning it into a club. Others want to keep it as it is. I like it small enough that I know most people's names. I'm thinking about closing new invites for a while.
description.culture: Grease under your fingernails, tea on the bench, no stupid questions. Fix it yourself if you can; ask for help if you can't.

communities.notes: Yusuf's personal space that has quietly become a community. He has absolute control and doesn't want more responsibility; regulars who see it as theirs too may be upset if he closes invites.

communities.name: Grandpa Joe

description.purpose: This group was where we shared updates while Grandpa Joe was in hospice. He passed peacefully on March 3rd, surrounded by family. We're keeping the group open as a place to share memories, photos and stories about him, and to keep the family connected the way he always wanted.
description.culture: Please be gentle with each other; everyone grieves differently. Aunt Carol and Mike are the admins. Questions about the estate and the house should go to Carol directly, not here.

communities.notes: About 50 relatives on Facebook. The group is changing purpose from crisis updates to memorial to general family group, and the estate disagreements everyone has been told to keep out keep leaking in through passive-aggressive comments.

communities.name: Night Owls

description.purpose: Games after midnight.

communities.notes: Five friends who met in an online game years ago and have never met in person. No rules, no admin roles; one of them pays for the server's boosts.

communities.name: Ruiru Estate Security

description.purpose: Security group for residents of the estate. Report suspicious people or vehicles, break-ins, power and water outages, and road issues. The estate committee also posts updates about the guards, gate rules and monthly security fees here.
description.culture: Report facts, not rumours. Include time and location. No forwards, no politics, no selling. Pay your security levy on time; the guards depend on it.

communities.notes: About 300 households with an elected estate committee. Posts about 'suspicious' young men walking through often turn out to be workers from the neighbouring village, which causes friction the committee rarely addresses.

communities.name: Eastgate Ward Forum

description.purpose:
The Eastgate Ward Forum is an online space for people who live, work or study in Eastgate ward to discuss local issues, share ideas and have a say in decisions that affect our area. It's hosted on the city council's engagement platform, but it's run by residents.

How it came about: in 2022 the council started a pilot to give each ward a small annual budget (£50,000 in Eastgate) for local projects chosen by residents, and set up forums on its platform for each ward. In most wards the forums are run by council officers. In Eastgate, residents asked to run it themselves, and the council agreed to try it.

Who does what:
- The council hosts the platform, provides an officer who answers questions about council services, and is responsible for spending the ward budget according to residents' decisions (as long as they're legal and within council policy).
- A volunteer residents' team of eight moderates the forum, organises the yearly budget process, and runs two in-person meetings a year at the community centre. The team is chosen at the spring meeting; anyone who lives in the ward can stand.
- Our two ward councillors take part like other members and report back on council decisions, but they don't moderate.

The budget process: in autumn, anyone can propose a project. The residents' team checks proposals with the council officer for feasibility. In February, everyone in the ward aged 14 and over can vote online or on paper at the library. Projects with the most votes are funded until the money runs out.

Forum rules:
- Be respectful. Disagree with ideas, not people.
- No party political campaigning (councillors can talk about their work, not their party).
- Complaints about specific council services go to the council's complaints system, not the forum. We'll help you find it.
- No personal details about other residents.

The current issue: the council is consulting on a new housing development on the old bus depot site. Many residents want to use the forum to organise opposition. The council says the forum shouldn't be used for campaigns against council decisions, and that it may have to step in to moderate. The residents' team thinks the forum belongs to residents and should be able to discuss anything that affects the ward. We're talking to the council about it now.
description.culture: A place for everyone in Eastgate: long-time residents, newcomers, students, young people. Let's disagree well and get things done.

communities.notes: About 1,200 members. It's both a council engagement tool and a residents' neighbourhood forum, and the depot dispute is testing who it really belongs to.

communities.name: Sunline Depot Drivers

description.purpose: Group for drivers at the Sunline depot. Route changes, roster updates, breakdowns, traffic and protest alerts, and shift swaps. Supervisors post official notices; drivers share what's happening on the road.
description.culture: Keep it about work and road conditions. Respect each other and the supervisors. If you have a complaint, raise it with your shop steward, not here. Stay safe out there.

communities.notes: About 80 drivers and three supervisors. The union shop steward is a member and quietly influential; drivers watch what they say because supervisors are in the group.

communities.name: Archivists Without Archives

description.purpose: A list for archivists who are unemployed, freelance, on short contracts, or otherwise between institutions.
description.culture: Commiserate, share leads, keep your skills sharp.

communities.notes: About 700 subscribers, run by one volunteer who set it up after a wave of layoffs. Low traffic, high trust; quietly important when jobs come up.

communities.name: Kita Marienkäfer (Ladybird Kindergarten)

description.purpose: Ladybird is a parent-run kindergarten (Elterninitiative) in Freiburg-Wiehre for 25 children aged 1–6. The parents are the association that runs the Kita: we hire the educators, manage the budget, and share the work, from cooking duty to garden days to bookkeeping. Signal is for day-to-day coordination; decisions are made at the monthly parents' evening.
description.culture: We decide together, by consensus. Every family has a voice, and we keep talking until everyone can live with the decision. That takes time, and we think it's worth it. The educators take part in parents' evenings and have the final say on everyday educational matters.
