communities.notes: About 25 families. A childcare setting where you'd expect professionals to decide, but parents run everything by consensus; decisions like hiring take months, and educators sometimes feel they work for 40 bosses.

communities.name: Agua Es Vida (Water Is Life)

description.purpose:
Water Is Life brings together neighbourhood water committees, irrigation farmers, students and residents of Cochabamba and the surrounding valley to defend water as a common good. We were born out of the memory of the Water War of 2000, when the people of Cochabamba drove out a private company that had taken over our water. Today our struggles are different: wells drying up, factories polluting the river, new housing developments with no water plans, and committees in the southern zone that have built their own water systems without any help from the state.

What we do:
- Support neighbourhood water committees with technical advice, legal help and connections
- Monitor the river and wells, with volunteers testing water quality
- Pressure the municipality and the departmental government through assemblies, marches and dialogue tables
- Train young people in water rights and community organisation

How we organise:
- The general assembly is the highest authority. It meets every two months, alternating between the southern zone, the centre and the valley. Each water committee, irrigators' association and collective sends delegates, but anyone can attend and speak.
- The assembly elects a coordinating committee of seven for one year, with rotation between zones. The coordinating committee carries out the assembly's decisions and represents the movement.
- Working groups (legal, technical, communications, youth) report to the assembly.
- WhatsApp groups: one for delegates, one for each working group, and one public announcements group with about 5,000 people.

Rules of the announcements group: only the communications group posts. For questions, write to the numbers in the description.

What we're going through: at the last assembly there was a hard debate. A political party offered to include several of our leaders on its list for the municipal elections, promising a water law. Some compañeros believe this is the chance to change things from inside. Others remember how other movements were divided and co-opted. The assembly decided that the movement will not support any party, and that anyone who runs for office must step down from the coordinating committee. Two members of the committee resigned to run. It hurt. We're still talking about it, in the neighbourhoods and the assemblies.
description.culture: Water is not a commodity. We decide in assembly, from below, and no party speaks for us. Respect for the elders who fought in 2000, and room for the young ones who will carry it forward.

communities.notes: About 5,000 people in the announcement group but a few hundred active delegates and volunteers. Its assembly structure is deep-rooted, and the party question has opened a real split between pragmatists and autonomists.

communities.name: Lofoten Cold Water Surfers

description.purpose: For surfers in Lofoten and northern Norway, locals and visitors. Share forecasts, conditions, car pools to Unstad and Flakstad, and gear for sale. Visitors: ask here before you go out, because conditions change fast and the water is cold.
description.culture: Respect the locals and the lineup. Leave nothing behind. Never surf alone in winter. Parking on farmers' land is not ok; use the official spots.

communities.notes: About 400 members, a mix of a few dozen local surfers and many tourists. The admins are locals who are protective of their breaks, and some newcomers find the vibe unfriendly.

communities.name: LibreFonts Hub

description.purpose: Open-source fonts for every script, under the SIL Open Font License.

communities.notes: About 150 contributors with a review committee of type designers who approve each family, and long debates about quality standards for under-resourced scripts. None of that appears in the one-liner.

communities.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Youth London

description.purpose: Telegram group for the youth fellowship (Sunday school) of our church in London. We share announcements for services, Bible study on Friday evenings, choir practice for the youth mezmur team, and preparations for Timket, Fasika and other holy days. Also a place to support each other in faith.
description.culture: Speak with respect, as you would in church. Amharic and English are both welcome. Posts should be about our faith and fellowship. Please obey the guidance of our Abba (priest) and the youth leaders.

communities.notes: About 90 young people aged 15–30. Led by elected youth leaders under the priest's authority. Second-generation members want more English and more discussion; leaders want to preserve tradition and Ge'ez.

communities.name: Adolescent Sleep Study

description.purpose:
This Teams space is for members of the Adolescent Sleep Study consortium: researchers, research assistants and students across our six sites in the UK, Netherlands, Norway, South Africa, Brazil and Australia. We're running a longitudinal study of sleep, mental health and school performance in about 4,000 adolescents, aged 12–18, using wearables, questionnaires and interviews.

Channels:
- General: announcements from the coordinating team
- Data: questions about the shared dataset, data dictionary, and the data access process
- Protocols: the study protocol, standard operating procedures, and amendments
- Site leads: private channel for the six site leads and the coordinating team
- Early career researchers: run by and for students and postdocs
- Papers: proposals and progress

Governance:
- The steering committee (one lead from each site plus the principal investigator at the coordinating site) makes decisions about the study, by majority vote. It meets monthly.
- Data access: all consortium members can use the shared dataset once their proposal is approved by the publications committee. Proposals must be posted in the Papers channel for two weeks so others can flag overlap.
- Authorship: the consortium's authorship policy applies. Each site that contributed data to a paper can nominate up to two authors. Early career researchers should be first authors on papers they lead. 'ASS Consortium' is listed as a group author on all papers. (Yes, we know about the acronym.)
- Ethics: each site follows its own ethics approval. Never upload identifiable participant data to Teams.

Current challenge: the Brazil and South Africa sites have raised concerns that most first-author papers so far have come from the European sites, which have more funding for analysis staff. They've proposed reserving some analysis topics for researchers from sites with less funding, and funding a data analyst for those sites from the shared budget. The steering committee is discussing this, and the early career researchers have prepared a statement supporting the proposal.
description.culture: Collaborative, rigorous and respectful across disciplines and countries. We're all in this because we care about young people's wellbeing.

communities.notes: About 45 members across six countries. Formal governance hides real inequality between rich and less-funded sites; the authorship dispute is about who benefits from data everyone collected.

communities.name: Seagrass Spotters

description.purpose: Seagrass Spotters maps seagrass meadows around the UK coast. Snorkellers, kayakers, divers and walkers upload photos and locations through our app, helping scientists and conservationists protect these vital habitats. The Facebook group is for sharing sightings, getting help with identification, and organising survey days.
description.culture: The university funding for the project ended in September, and the research team has moved on, but the app and the data are staying online, and a group of volunteers is keeping things going. We're working out how. Please bear with us, and get in touch if you'd like to help.

communities.notes: About 700 volunteers. The research team used to verify records and run everything; now five volunteers have inherited it, with no clear authority, unclear data ownership, and an app they don't know how to maintain.

communities.name: Kaffeeklatsch

description.purpose: Germany's living room since 2001. Everything goes, except bad manners.

communities.notes: About 30,000 accounts, run by a two-person admin team and a dozen moderators. The 'bad manners' rule is enforced quite strictly, especially in the politics sub-forum.

communities.name: MedPeers Manila

description.purpose: Peer support Discord for medical students in Metro Manila. Talk about exams, duty hours, toxic residents, money worries, and the feeling that everyone else is coping better than you. We also have study rooms, and channels for board exam prep.
description.culture: No flexing grades. No judgment. What happens in the vent channel stays there. If you're in crisis, reach out to the mods and the resources pinned in every channel. You're not alone, doc.

communities.notes: About 600 members across several schools. Run by student mods without professional supervision; they sometimes handle serious mental health situations beyond their training.

communities.name: Hillside Childcare Co-op

description.purpose:
Hillside is a parent cooperative preschool in Portland for children aged 2 to 5. We've been running since 1974 in the basement of the Hillside community church (we're not affiliated with the church; we rent the space). We have one professional teacher, our director Ms. Ruth, and the rest of the teaching is done by parents.

How it works:
- Each family works one morning a week in the classroom as an assistant teacher, alongside Ms. Ruth. You'll get training before you start, and Ms. Ruth guides the day.
- Each family also has a job in the co-op: treasurer, enrollment, maintenance, snack coordinator, fundraising, etc. Jobs are assigned at the start of the year.
- Tuition is much lower than other preschools, because of the work families put in.
- Parents attend a monthly meeting with a parent education talk and co-op business.

Governance: the co-op is a nonprofit owned by its member families. A parent board of seven, elected each spring, makes decisions about the budget, policies and hiring. Each family has one vote at general meetings, which approve the budget and any major changes. Ms. Ruth has authority over everything to do with the curriculum and the classroom.

Communication: the email list is for co-op business and announcements; the rota spreadsheet shows classroom days. Please email Ms. Ruth directly about your child.

The current challenge: more families now have two parents working full time, and finding a weekday morning has become very hard. Some families have been paying a fee instead of working a shift, which the board allowed as an exception. Now a third of families do it, and some parents feel this is turning Hillside into a regular preschool where wealthier families buy out of the work. The board has proposed limiting buy-outs to ten families, chosen by need. This goes to a general meeting vote next month.
description.culture: We raise our kids together. Parents learn as much as the children do. Come with patience, a sense of humour, and clothes you don't mind getting paint on.

communities.notes: About 30 families. A school and a co-op at once: parents are both customers and teachers, and the buy-out debate is about whether the co-op model survives modern work patterns.

communities.name: Tbilisi Hash House Harriers

description.purpose: A drinking club with a running problem, Tbilisi chapter. Every Saturday a hare lays a trail through the city or the hills, the pack follows it, and then we drink, sing, and give people silly names. Runners, walkers, expats, locals, all welcome.
description.culture: No rules, except: don't take it seriously, don't be a jerk, and don't call it a race. The Grand Master's decision is final, and is usually wrong.

communities.notes: About 80 members, mostly expats and a growing number of Georgians. Hash traditions (ritual roles like Grand Master, mock trials, drinking songs) form a real if playful governance system that newcomers have to learn.

communities.name: Romani Voices

description.purpose: Romani culture, history, music and news, told by Roma.

communities.notes: About 2,000 followers on Instagram, run by a collective of young Romani activists in several European countries. Comments sections attract racist trolls; the team spends much of its time deleting them.

communities.name: Amaka's Book Club

description.purpose: The official book club from Amaka Reads! Every month Amaka announces a book in her video, we read along, and discuss here on Discord chapter by chapter. At the end of the month she hosts a live discussion. Mostly African and diaspora authors, with some wild cards.
description.culture: Read at your own pace. Spoiler channels for each section. Disagree about books, not about people. And yes, Amaka reads the threads (sometimes).

communities.notes: About 4,000 members. Amaka picks the books and does the monthly live, but rarely posts; the day-to-day discussion is run by a few super-readers. Members treat it like a real book club and resent that the creator controls the choices without being involved.

communities.name: Fjord Protocol DAO

description.purpose:
Fjord Protocol is a decentralized lending protocol. FJORD token holders govern the protocol: risk parameters, new assets, the treasury, and protocol upgrades. This Discourse is the official governance forum; Snapshot is used for off-chain signalling and on-chain votes are executed through the Governor contract.

Governance process:
1. Temperature check: post in the Proposals category using the template. Discussion runs for at least 5 days.
2. Snapshot vote: requires support from a delegate with at least 100,000 FJORD of voting power. Runs for 5 days, 3% quorum.
3. On-chain vote: passed Snapshot proposals become on-chain proposals. 4% quorum, 2-day timelock before execution.

Delegates: most token holders delegate their votes. Delegates post a platform and are expected to explain their votes publicly. There are currently about 60 active delegates; the top 10 hold about 70% of delegated voting power.

Risk council: an elected council of five risk experts can adjust certain risk parameters (like collateral factors) within set limits, without a full vote, to respond quickly to market conditions. Its decisions are published within 24 hours and can be overturned by a governance vote.

Emergency council: a 4-of-7 multisig can pause the protocol in an emergency, such as an exploit. It cannot move funds. Members are elected annually.

Service providers: the DAO pays several companies (including the original developers) for development, risk analysis and security. Their contracts are renewed by governance vote every year.

Forum rules: no price talk, no shilling, no personal attacks. Disclose conflicts of interest: if you or your company would benefit from a proposal, say so.

Ongoing discussion: this year's renewal of the main development contract, worth several million dollars, is being debated. Critics say the original developers have too much influence, as both service provider and large delegates. Supporters say no one else knows the code as well. Several delegates have proposed splitting the contract among multiple teams.
description.culture: Professional, transparent, focused on the long-term health of the protocol. Good governance is boring, and that's a good thing.

communities.notes: About 9,000 forum members but real decisions sit with a few dozen delegates, several of whom are companies paid by the DAO. Looks like a functioning democracy; works more like an oligarchy with elaborate procedure.

communities.name: Theo's Thoughts

description.purpose: Started as my server for posting my thoughts at people. Now it's twenty of us posting thoughts at each other. Music, memes, Leeds, life.
description.culture: Every Monday the server gets a new King (or Queen, or Monarch). The current King has owner powers for the week: they can rename channels, set the theme, make a silly rule (last week: all messages must end in 'mate'), and settle arguments. The King picks the next King by Sunday night. You can't be King twice in a row. Theo has reserve powers in case someone deletes everything, but has promised not to use them except for that.

communities.notes: Twenty friends and friends-of-friends. A personal space turned into a deliberate experiment in rotating power. It's fun and keeps things fresh, but some quieter members never get picked, and the 'reserve powers' have never been tested.

communities.name: Okeke Twins

description.purpose: Photos and updates on Chidera and Chiamaka for family and friends 💕

communities.notes: About 30 relatives and close friends. The parents are the only admins and posters; everyone else replies with heart emojis and prayers.

communities.name: Ladies Who Lunch (Badly)

description.purpose: Six women, one lunch a month, somewhere in Joburg. Whoever's turn it is picks the place and books it. Also used for birthday reminders, gossip, and moral support during divorces, menopause and teenagers.
description.culture: What's said at lunch stays at lunch. If you cancel less than a day before, you pay for the wine next time.

communities.notes: Six friends in their 50s who met through their children's school. No formal roles, but one member keeps the rota and reminds everyone, and is getting a bit tired of it.

communities.name: Saltmarsh Lane Flood Group

description.purpose:
We're the residents of Saltmarsh Lane, the Creek Road estate and Mill Close, in the lower part of the village, which floods. We set this group up after the December 2020 floods, when 34 homes flooded and it took the council three days to bring sandbags.

What we've done since then:
- Made a flood plan for the area, including a phone tree to wake people up at night if the water is rising
- Bought (with a grant) our own stock of flood barriers and sandbags, stored in the Wilsons' garage at number 12
- Trained 15 flood wardens who check the gauges and the drains when heavy rain is forecast
- Pushed the Environment Agency and the council to clear the culvert under Mill Lane, which they finally did last year
- Helped flooded families with insurance claims and finding builders

How we work: anyone living in the flood area can join. We meet in the village hall every couple of months, and the WhatsApp group is for quick updates and flood alerts. A steering group of five (Pat, Graham, Shazia, Dave and Lucy) keeps things moving between meetings. We've never had a constitution or elections; people just stepped up.

What's changing: we've been offered a big grant, £80,000 over three years, to install property flood resilience measures in every house and take on a part-time coordinator. To get it, we need to become a registered charity: a constitution, elected trustees, annual accounts, safeguarding policies, the lot. A local community foundation has offered to help us do it.

Some people are thrilled. Others worry that we'll turn into a committee full of paperwork, that the people who do the work on flood nights will be pushed aside by people who are good at meetings, or that we'll start fighting about money. We're having a special meeting on 14th March to decide whether to go ahead, and if so, how to keep what's good about us.
description.culture: Neighbours looking out for neighbours. When the water comes, nobody is on their own. Everyone pulls their weight, and everyone has a say.

communities.notes: About 120 households, with a steering group that emerged naturally. Formalising as a charity would bring money but also elections and paperwork, and may shift power away from the people who wade through floodwater.

communities.name: Bath Neighbourhood Planning Forum

description.purpose: We're the designated neighbourhood forum for our area of Bath, preparing a neighbourhood plan that will shape new development, green spaces, transport and heritage protection for the next 15 years. Once approved in a local referendum, the plan becomes part of the legal planning framework. Join to comment on draft policies, come to workshops, or join a topic group.
description.culture: Open to everyone who lives, works or runs a business in the area. We want to hear from people who don't usually come to meetings: renters, students, young families. The forum committee is elected at our AGM.

communities.notes: About 400 members, but the committee is mostly retired homeowners with planning or architecture backgrounds. Students and renters are hard to reach and the draft policies lean toward preserving the status quo.

communities.name: Cuadrilla de Vendimia (Harvest Crew)

description.purpose: Harvest crew group: start times, which vineyard block, transport, and pay days.

communities.notes: About 50 seasonal workers, many from Bolivia and northern Argentina, and the crew boss who is the only admin. Pay is per bin, and disputes over counts are handled off the chat.

communities.name: Freelance Sound Engineers Japan

description.purpose: For freelance live sound, recording and post-production engineers working in Japan. Topics: consoles (Yamaha CL/QL/Rivage, DiGiCo, Avid), PA systems and rigging, in-ear monitor setups, Dante networks, festival and venue specs, DAW workflows, and gear for sale. Gig requests in #jobs.

communities.notes: About 800 members, with a strong seniority culture where veteran engineers set the tone and newcomers rarely challenge them. Talk of rates and unpaid overtime happens in DMs. The description only lists gear and topics.

communities.name: Bootcamp Cohort 14

description.purpose:
Welcome to Cohort 14! This Slack is home for the next 16 weeks of the full-stack web development bootcamp. You'll find your schedule, assignments, and resources here, and it's where you'll get help from instructors, mentors and, most of all, each other.

Channels:
- #announcements: from the instructors only. Check it every morning.
- #help: stuck? Post your question with the error, what you've tried, and a code snippet. Use threads.
- #pair-up: daily pair programming assignments are posted here.
- #standup: post your daily standup by 9:30 (yesterday, today, blockers).
- #projects: share your projects for feedback.
- #random: memes, lunch plans, everything else.
- #jobs: from week 10, career coaching and job leads.

How help works: try for 20 minutes on your own, then ask your pair, then post in #help. Mentors (graduates of earlier cohorts) answer during the day; instructors run office hours from 3 to 5.

Pair programming rules:
- The driver types, the navigator thinks. Switch every 25 minutes.
- Be patient with your pair; you'll both be the slower one sometimes.
- If a pairing really isn't working, tell an instructor privately.

Academic honesty: you'll learn by writing your own code. Copying code from classmates, or submitting AI-generated projects as your own work, isn't allowed. Using AI as a tutor is fine; using it to do the assignment is not. Second offence means you can't graduate.

What happened in week 6: two projects were submitted that were nearly identical, and it turned out one student had shared their whole repo in a DM. Both students had a conversation with the program lead, and both had to redo the project. Several of you asked where the line is between helping and cheating. Here's our answer: talk about approaches, share error messages, help someone debug. Don't share working solutions before the deadline. If you're unsure, ask.
description.culture: Everyone here started at zero not long ago. Be generous, ask lots of questions, and celebrate each other's wins. Imposter syndrome is normal; quitting isn't the only option.

communities.notes: About 35 adult career-changers paying significant fees, plus instructors and mentors. The plagiarism incident made a supportive, collaborative culture tense, and students who are falling behind are now afraid to ask for help.

communities.name: Grève Climat Montréal (Montréal Climate Strike)

description.purpose: We're high school and CEGEP students in Montréal striking for the climate. We organise school strikes and marches, push school boards and the government for real climate action and climate education, and support students who get punished for striking. Follow us on Instagram for actions; join the Signal group to help organise.
description.culture: Led by students, for students. Decisions are made at our general assemblies, where every student who comes gets a vote. Adults are welcome as allies, but they don't lead. Respect, inclusion, and zero tolerance for harassment.

communities.notes: About 1,200 followers and a core of 30 or so organisers. It turns over every year as students graduate, so knowledge is constantly lost, and a few CEGEP students effectively run it between assemblies.

communities.name: Birdsong Recording Gear

description.purpose: Shotgun mics, parabolic reflectors, handheld recorders, wind protection and settings for recording birdsong in the field.

communities.notes: A forum of about 3,000 members that also has strong norms about not disturbing nesting birds and not using playback, enforced by the moderators. None of that appears in the gear-only description.

communities.name: OpenRecipes Commons

description.purpose: A free, openly licensed collection of recipes from home cooks around the world, structured as data so anyone can build apps, tools and research on top of it. Add your family recipe, translate one, test one and report back, or help clean the data (units, ingredient names, allergens).
description.culture: Every cuisine is welcome, and every grandmother is an authority. Credit where recipes come from. Don't copy recipes from cookbooks or websites; write your own version. Edits are reviewed by experienced editors.

communities.notes: About 500 contributors. The editor team is mostly North American and European, and arguments about what makes a dish 'authentic' versus 'adapted' sometimes get heated around recipes from other cultures.

communities.name: Dhikr Circle Üsküdar

description.purpose:
This is the group of our dhikr circle in Üsküdar. We meet every Thursday evening after the night prayer, in our lodge near the waterfront, for remembrance of God (dhikr), recitation of the Qur'an, and conversation (sohbet) with our sheikh. The circle has met in this neighbourhood, in one form or another, for more than a hundred years.

This WhatsApp group is for:
- Announcements of gatherings, holy nights and special programs
- The text of the weekly wird (litany) and readings
- Requests for prayers for the sick and the departed
- Practical organisation: who is bringing food, who will open the lodge

For those who are new: you are welcome to come and sit with us. Come with ablution, dress modestly, and sit quietly for the first gatherings. Men and women sit in separate parts of the lodge. Do not record or photograph the gatherings. If you wish to take the path, speak with one of the elder dervishes, who will bring you to the sheikh.

In the group: please do not forward messages from outside, do not argue about politics or other groups, and do not share the sheikh's words outside without permission. Questions about practice should be asked to the elders privately, not in the group.

Since the pandemic, the sheikh has allowed some of the sohbet to be shared as voice recordings for brothers and sisters abroad. This has brought new people from Germany, the Netherlands and the US into the group. Some of the elders feel that the path is transmitted in person, heart to heart, and that recordings and a growing online group change its nature. The sheikh has said he will reflect on it, and we wait for his guidance.
description.culture: Adab (good manners) before everything. Humility, service and remembrance. Speak little, listen much.

communities.notes: About 70 members, with a sheikh whose authority is complete and unquestioned, and elder dervishes as gatekeepers. The online growth question is a conflict between tradition and reach, which only the sheikh can resolve.

communities.name: ALS Open Research

description.purpose: People living with ALS, caregivers, and researchers working together. We track our own symptoms and treatments with shared tools, discuss new papers in plain language, help design questions for studies, and connect patients with trials. Some of our patient-collected data has been used in published research.
description.culture: Patients are experts in their own disease. Researchers here listen as much as they explain. Share data only with consent. No miracle cures or selling. Be gentle; many of us are running out of time.

communities.notes: About 300 members on Discord. Half a patient support group, half a research collaboration, so grief and science share a space, and researchers' publication timelines feel unbearably slow to patients.

communities.name: Frog Call Survey NSW

description.purpose: Record frog calls on your phone and help map frogs across New South Wales.

communities.notes: About 1,500 volunteers. A museum's expert team identifies every recording, and volunteers mostly just upload and get an ID back.

communities.name: Chai Point

description.purpose: India's chillest hangout server. Chat, gaming, cricket, Bollywood and anime, study VCs for JEE and NEET aspirants, and regional channels for every state. Weekly events: antakshari nights, cricket watch parties, game tournaments.
description.culture: Respect everyone, whatever their state, language or religion. No politics or communal content, ever. No NSFW. Staff are volunteers; open a ticket if there's a problem.

communities.notes: About 22,000 members, mostly teenagers and students, with a large staff ranked by level. The 'no politics' rule is constantly tested and staff themselves don't always agree on what counts as political.

communities.name: Many Voices Peer Circle

description.purpose:
Many Voices is an online peer support forum for people who hear voices, see visions, or have other unusual sensory experiences, whatever they call them and however they understand them. Some of us have a diagnosis like schizophrenia, psychosis or bipolar disorder; some of us don't; some of us reject diagnosis altogether. Some of us take medication; some don't. All of that is welcome here.

We started in 2015 as a small group of people who'd met at in-person hearing voices groups and wanted something available at 3am. Now we're about 2,000 members around the world.

What makes us different: this forum is run entirely by peers, people with lived experience of voices. There are no psychiatrists, psychologists or other professionals moderating. That's deliberate. Many of us have felt unheard, disbelieved or controlled by services, and we wanted a place where our experiences are taken seriously on our own terms. Professionals are welcome to read and learn, but they post as individuals, not as experts.

Our values:
- Your experience is real to you, and you are the expert on it.
- There's no single right way to understand voices: spiritual, psychological, medical, trauma-related, or something else.
- We don't tell anyone to stop or start medication. We support people to make their own informed decisions.
- We share coping strategies, not instructions.

Forum rules:
1. No telling anyone their understanding of their voices is wrong.
2. Don't post detailed content of distressing voices without a content warning.
3. Don't share anyone's posts outside the forum.
4. If you're in danger or thinking of harming yourself or someone else, please contact local emergency services or a crisis line. Our crisis resources page lists them by country. Peers can be with you while you reach out.

How it's run: a team of nine peer moderators, all of whom hear voices or have done, chosen by the existing team. Moderators get training and regular peer supervision from each other. Decisions about the forum's direction are discussed openly in the Members' Lounge.

The hard part: being peer-only means we sometimes face situations, like someone in acute crisis, that feel beyond us. We hold to our approach, but we've been discussing whether to bring in a professional adviser behind the scenes, not as a moderator. Many members strongly oppose it.
description.culture: Belief, respect and curiosity. Come as you are; we've heard stranger things, sometimes literally.

communities.notes: Deliberately peer-led and grounded in the hearing voices movement, which values members' own interpretations over medical ones. The professional-adviser question is identity-defining, and moderators carry a heavy emotional load.

communities.name: Atelier Partagé (Shared Workshop)

description.purpose: A cooperative woodworking and metalworking workshop in Lyon's 7th arrondissement. Members share the space, the machines (table saw, planer, lathe, MIG welder) and the cost. Book machine time on Discord, sign up for safety training, and join our monthly members' meeting.
description.culture: No one uses a machine without training: no exceptions. Clean up after yourself. Share your knowledge. Big decisions (new machines, fees, new members) are made at the monthly meeting, one member one vote.

communities.notes: About 45 members. A few highly skilled members do all the trainings and maintenance and have outsized influence; disagreements about who keeps the space clean never really end.

communities.name: Uppsala Go Club

description.purpose: We play Go at the university library café on Tuesday evenings. Beginners welcome; boards provided.

communities.notes: About 30 on the email list, a dozen regulars, mostly students and a few long-time locals. One player organises everything and has done so for 15 years.

communities.name: Gamers Surdos BR (Deaf Gamers Brazil)

description.purpose: A community for Deaf and hard-of-hearing gamers in Brazil. Find teammates who communicate the way you do, talk about accessibility in games (subtitles, visual cues, Libras in streams), and play together without voice chat pressure. We also push studios and tournaments to be more accessible.
description.culture: Here, Deaf culture comes first. Libras is welcome in video, Portuguese in text. Hearing people who are learning Libras are welcome as allies. No mocking anyone's writing; for many of us Portuguese is a second language.

communities.notes: About 1,200 members. Half a Deaf identity community, half a gaming group; fierce debates about whether hearing members and oral (non-signing) deaf people fully belong.

communities.name: The Quiet Market

description.purpose:
Welcome to The Quiet Market, the community for Haneul's ASMR channel. Haneul makes calm roleplay and sound videos (the market stall series, rainy library, late-night tea shop), and this is where listeners gather to share sleep routines, favourite triggers, fan art, and kindness.

About 20,000 of you are here now. That's a lot of people who need a quiet place.

Channels:
- #announcements: new uploads and streams
- #requests: suggest sounds and scenarios. Haneul reads them, but can't do them all.
- #sleep-club: who's awake, what are you listening to?
- #fanart and #creations
- #wind-down: a slow channel (one message per 10 minutes) for those who want gentle chat before bed
- #members-lounge: for YouTube channel members

Rules (please read; we take them seriously):
1. Respect Haneul's privacy. Do not try to find or share personal information, real name, address, face (if not shown), or family details. Do not speculate about her personal life or relationships. Breaking this rule means an immediate permanent ban.
2. No sexual content or comments about Haneul or anyone else.
3. Haneul is a creator, not your friend or partner. She cares about this community, but she can't reply to DMs. Please don't send gifts to anything other than official channels.
4. ASMR is personal. Never mock anyone's triggers or why they listen.
5. No content about self-harm in public channels; see the pinned support resources.

Moderation: the mod team (eight people from different time zones, chosen by Haneul and the head mod, Jiwoo) enforces these rules. Haneul has the final say.

Why rule 1 is so strict: in the spring, someone posted a photo they claimed showed Haneul's apartment building, figured out from reflections in a video. It was removed within minutes, but it spread to other sites. Haneul took a two-month break and moved. She's back now and doing well, and asked us to say plainly: please protect each other's privacy, and hers.
description.culture: Soft, safe and slow. Like the last hour of a night market, when everyone speaks quietly.

communities.notes: A large creator community with intense parasocial attachment. After the doxxing scare, moderation is strict and the creator is more distant, which some long-time listeners experience as being shut out.

communities.name: Mangrove Restoration DAO

description.purpose: We fund community-led mangrove restoration in Indonesia, Kenya, Madagascar and Colombia. Members vote on which local groups receive funding, and each project shares photos, planting data and satellite images so we can watch the forests grow. Join the Discord to follow projects and take part in governance.
description.culture: Local communities know their coasts best; we fund them, we don't direct them. Transparency about every dollar. Patience: mangroves take years.

communities.notes: About 600 members, almost all donors in rich countries voting on projects in poorer ones. The founders are working on giving partner communities a formal voice, but it hasn't happened yet.

communities.name: Kai's Rants

description.purpose: I rant. You listen. Sometimes you rant back.

communities.notes: A dozen friends on Kai's Discord. Entirely Kai's space; others mostly react with emojis.

communities.name: Familie Bakker

description.purpose: Our family planning hub: the shared calendar with everyone's sports, music lessons, work trips and visits to Oma, plus the Signal chat for who's cooking, who's picking up whom, and last-minute changes. Nine of us, including Opa and Oma, who joined last year (welcome!).
description.culture: If it's not in the calendar, it's not happening. Check before you ask. Reply to questions with a thumbs up so we know you saw it.

communities.notes: Two parents, four kids aged 8–17, and grandparents in Utrecht. Mum is the real organiser and the calendar's only admin; the teenagers constantly forget to update it.

communities.name: Book & Bottle

description.purpose:
We're ten friends in Dublin who've met once a month since 2016 to talk about a book and drink a bottle of wine (or three). It's always been at someone's flat, with the host choosing the book and cooking. The WhatsApp group is for picking dates, arguing about the book in advance, and general life updates.

Some things that have always just worked:
- Hosting rotates. The host picks the book, and nobody's allowed to complain about it more than once.
- If you haven't finished the book, you still come.
- No partners unless they're actually reading the book.

What's happened: Ciara and Rob, who were a couple and both founding members, broke up in the summer. It was a hard breakup. Since then, they haven't both been at the same meeting, and people have been tiptoeing around it. Some of us are closer to one of them than the other, and it's started to feel like sides.

Rob suggested the group just carry on and they'll manage. Ciara feels she can't come while Rob's there, and has suggested maybe splitting into two groups. Some people really don't want that. Others think it might be kinder for everyone.

We've agreed to take a break for a month and meet to talk about it, without either of them, to work out what we want, and then talk to them both. Nobody's in charge of this group, which has never mattered until now.
description.culture: Books, wine, honesty, and a lot of shouting about endings. We've been through a lot together. We'd like to keep it that way.

communities.notes: Ten friends with no formal structure facing a split triggered by a breakup. With no leader and no rules for conflict, the 'neutral' members having a meeting without the two people involved risks feeling like a tribunal.

communities.name: Jardim Comunitário da Graça (Graça Community Garden)

description.purpose: Our community garden on the empty lot behind Rua da Graça, created by neighbours in 2019 with permission from the parish council. We grow vegetables and herbs in shared and individual beds, compost neighbourhood food scraps, and hold a harvest lunch every September. This WhatsApp group is for watering rotas, work days, and sharing harvests.
description.culture: The garden belongs to everyone who looks after it. Water your bed, take part in work days, and share your extra tomatoes. Children and elders especially welcome. Disagreements are discussed at our monthly meeting on the bench under the fig tree.

communities.notes: About 70 members, a mix of older Portuguese neighbours and newer foreign residents. Waiting lists for individual beds and the rising number of foreigners in a gentrifying area cause quiet tension.

communities.name: Report It Kumasi

description.purpose: Report potholes, broken streetlights, blocked gutters and illegal dumping in Kumasi. We send it to the Assembly and track the response.

communities.notes: An app and WhatsApp line run by a civic-tech startup with an informal partnership with the Assembly. Residents report, but rarely see fixes, and the startup has no formal power.
communities.setupNotes: app plus WhatsApp line; format unclear

communities.name: Orbit Labs

description.purpose: Orbit Labs builds AI-powered logistics software for India's fast-growing quick commerce market. Our platform optimises dark store inventory, rider routing and delivery time prediction in real time, serving 12 of India's top quick commerce and grocery brands across 40 cities. We're backed by leading investors and growing fast.

communities.notes: This is the company's internal Slack of about 60 people, but the description is the marketing pitch. In reality, two founders make all decisions, there are long hours and frequent reorganisations, and a recent round of layoffs that nobody talks about openly.

communities.name: Women in Mining Peru

description.purpose:
Women in Mining Peru is a professional network for women working in the mining sector: geologists, engineers, metallurgists, operators, environmental and community relations specialists, and executives. We have about 2,500 members, across our LinkedIn group, our WhatsApp communities (by region and specialty) and our in-person chapters in Lima, Arequipa and Cajamarca.

What we do:
- A mentoring program pairing young professionals and students with experienced women in the industry, 120 pairs this year
- Advocacy for safety, including properly fitting personal protective equipment for women, adequate facilities at camps and sites, and zero tolerance for harassment
- Training workshops and an annual conference
- A job board and a scholarships program for women studying mining engineering and geology

How we're organised: we're a registered nonprofit association. Members elect a board of directors every two years; the current board has seven members. Regional chapters have their own coordinators. Our activities are funded by membership fees, and by sponsorship from mining companies and suppliers.

Rules for our groups:
- Professional respect. We come from different companies, roles and regions; we're all colleagues here.
- Confidential information about companies, projects or incidents should not be shared.
- Job posts must be for real positions and include the company name.
- Harassment experiences can be shared, but without naming individuals publicly. Our support committee can help privately.

The current discussion: last year we published a report on harassment and safety for women in mining camps, based on a member survey. Some sponsoring companies were unhappy with how it portrayed the industry, and one withdrew its sponsorship. Some members feel the board softened the final version to keep sponsors happy; the board says it made the report more rigorous. At our general assembly this month, members will vote on a proposal to cap the share of our budget that can come from any single company.
description.culture: Supportive, professional and brave. We celebrate each other's achievements, and we speak up for women who can't.

communities.notes: A well-organised professional network caught between advocating for members and depending on the companies they work for. Women from operations and camp roles feel the network is dominated by engineers and executives in Lima.

communities.name: Deutschkurs B1 Abendgruppe (Evening German B1)

description.purpose: WhatsApp group for the German B1 evening course at the adult education centre in Hamburg-Altona, Monday and Wednesday 18:00–21:00. Our teacher Frau Krüger posts homework and materials. We use it to ask questions, share notes when someone is absent, and practise German together.
description.culture: Please write in German when you can, even if it's not perfect. That's why we're here! Be patient and kind. No politics, no religion, no forwards.

communities.notes: 18 adult learners from Syria, Ukraine, Afghanistan, Turkey, Brazil and Vietnam, plus the teacher. Learners often switch into English or Arabic, and the teacher is torn between enforcing German and keeping people engaged.

communities.name: No to the Bypass

description.purpose: The proposed eastern bypass would destroy Fenwick Wood and cut the village in two. Say no.

communities.notes: About 1,500 members on Facebook. Run by a residents' action committee that hired a planning lawyer and holds strategy meetings in the pub, none of which is visible from the one-liner. Some villagers actually want the bypass and get abuse in the comments.

communities.name: Mahjong Aunties Ipoh

description.purpose: Mahjong kakis in Ipoh! We arrange tables at each other's houses or the clubhouse every week. Post when you want to play and how many you need. Beginners can join the Thursday afternoon table where we teach slowly.
description.culture: Friendly games only, small stakes or no stakes, your choice. No fighting over tiles. Bring snacks. Whoever hosts decides the house rules.

communities.notes: About 30 women aged 50–80, mostly retired. One auntie admin who knows everyone; disputes about house rules and slow players are settled by whoever's hosting.

communities.name: Atlas de Hablas (Atlas of Dialects)

description.purpose:
Atlas de Hablas is an open, collaborative atlas of the dialects and ways of speaking Spanish around the world. Contributors record speakers saying the same set of words and sentences, and answer questions about local vocabulary (what do you call a straw? a bus? a kite?), and we put it all on a map. The recordings and data are free for anyone to use, under an open licence: researchers, teachers, writers, and the just plain curious.

We have about 400 active contributors in 22 countries, and over 15,000 recordings, from Patagonia to New Mexico and from the Canary Islands to Equatorial Guinea.

How to contribute:
- Record: use our recording kit (word list, sentences and a short free story) with a speaker, who may be you. Upload the audio and the speaker's details (age, place, years lived there, other languages).
- Vocabulary: answer the questionnaires about your local words.
- Review: experienced contributors check new recordings for audio quality, completeness and correct metadata.
- Transcribe: help write down what speakers say in free stories.

Consent rules (very important):
- Every speaker must sign or record the consent form before recording. No consent, no upload.
- Speakers can ask for their recording to be removed at any time, and we will remove it.
- For speakers under 18, a parent or guardian must consent.
- Don't record anyone without their knowledge, ever.

Editorial review: all recordings are reviewed by a regional editor before publication. Regional editors are experienced contributors who know the variety well. Disagreements about classification (for example, which variety a recording belongs to) are discussed on the wiki talk pages.

The project is coordinated by a small team of linguists from three universities, who maintain the platform and the methodology, and a council of regional editors that decides questions about content.

Ongoing discussion: some contributors from Latin America and Equatorial Guinea have said the atlas's structure, which started with Spain's provinces and is very detailed there, makes their regions look like single blocks. They've proposed redesigning the map structure to be more balanced, which would be a lot of work. The council is discussing it.
description.culture: Every way of speaking is valuable. There's no 'correct' Spanish here, just Spanish as people really speak it. Respect speakers, their voices and their privacy.

communities.notes: About 400 contributors with strong consent norms and a two-tier governance (coordinating linguists, regional editors council). The map-structure debate reflects a deeper imbalance of whose varieties the project was designed around.

communities.name: Friends of Cloister Ales

description.purpose: A forum for friends of the abbey and lovers of the beer our community has brewed since 1872. Talk about tasting, cellaring and food pairings, and learn about the brewing tradition. You can also follow news from the abbey, prayer intentions, and retreat dates for those who wish to visit and share in the life of the monastery.
description.culture: We welcome everyone, believer or not, in the spirit of Benedictine hospitality. Please drink responsibly and speak charitably. Brother Anselm moderates on behalf of the community; the Abbot has the final word.

communities.notes: About 1,500 members, mostly beer enthusiasts, with a smaller group drawn by the spiritual side. It's a faith community's outreach, a hobby forum and a sales channel at once, and the monks are uneasy when the beer talk gets rowdy or commercial.

communities.name: Hydrogen Catalysis Lab

description.purpose: Lab channel: instrument bookings, safety notices, group meeting schedule.

communities.notes: About 15 researchers at a Dutch technical university with close industry funding ties. The PI decides priorities, often shaped by what the industry partner wants.

communities.name: Drift Counters

description.purpose: Help oceanographers understand the tiny life that feeds the ocean. Our underwater cameras take millions of images of plankton, and you can help identify and count them: diatoms, copepods, jellies, larvae and things we don't have names for yet. No experience needed. The forum is where volunteers and scientists discuss strange finds and results.
description.culture: Wonder, patience and care. Tag the weird ones! Scientists answer questions on Fridays.

communities.notes: About 4,000 volunteers, a few dozen of whom are deeply expert by now. Scientists set every rule, and the expert volunteers want to be able to validate others' classifications, which the team hasn't allowed.

communities.name: Café Babel

description.purpose:
Café Babel is a multilingual discussion forum where people from everywhere talk about anything: politics, books, food, science, everyday life. We have sections in 14 languages and a shared 'Babel' area where posts are written in your own language and translated by members. About 10,000 members in more than 100 countries.

We're invitation-only, and we're very deliberate about it.

How you join: an existing member who has been here at least a year invites you, and becomes your sponsor. Your sponsor introduces you in the Welcome Hall, and is responsible for helping you learn how things work here. If you break the rules seriously in your first year, your sponsor loses invitation rights for a year too. Each member can sponsor at most two people a year.

Why: we started in 2012 as an open forum, and by 2016 we were overrun by trolls, spam and nationalist brawls. We closed sign-ups, tried invitations, and found that sponsorship worked better than any moderation system. People behave when someone they know vouched for them.

Rules:
1. Write as if the person reading is from the country you're arguing about. Often they are.
2. No dehumanising language about any nationality, ethnicity, religion or group.
3. In the Babel area, write in your own language. Help translate when you can. Mistranslating on purpose is a serious offence.
4. Disagreement is welcome. Contempt is not.
5. One account per person, real or consistent pseudonym.

Governance: an elected council of nine members, chosen by all members every year, sets policy. A team of about 40 volunteer moderators, covering all language sections, enforces it. The founders are members like everyone else, though one of them still pays the server bills.

Current debate: some members argue that invitation-only has made Café Babel too comfortable, too educated, and too European, and that we're no longer hearing the voices we most need to. They want an open 'guest house' section where anyone can read and post with limits. Others fear it would bring back the problems of 2016. The council is preparing a referendum.
description.culture: Curious, courteous, cosmopolitan. A café where you can argue with a stranger from the other side of the world and still share a table afterwards.

communities.notes: A big general social space with a membership model more typical of small private clubs. It's civil and high-quality, but exclusive in ways that track class and education, which the 'guest house' debate is really about.

communities.name: Papás Solos Lima (Single Dads Lima)

description.purpose: A group for fathers in Lima who are raising their children alone or sharing custody. Share advice on everything from school paperwork to doing your daughter's hair, legal questions about custody and child support, and organise weekend outings with the kids. And sometimes just talk, because nobody else asks how we're doing.
description.culture: No judging and no macho attitudes. Asking for help is a sign of strength. We don't speak badly about the mothers of our children in this group. Kids come first.

communities.notes: About 150 members. Founded by a father who went through a bitter custody case; the 'no badmouthing mothers' rule is the one most often broken, and he deletes posts himself.

communities.name: Solar Sisters Co-op

description.purpose: Women in Mzuzu selling solar lamps and chargers together. Orders, stock and meetings.

communities.notes: About 80 members with an elected chairlady and treasurer. Started with NGO support that has since ended, and most business is done at the Saturday meeting, with WhatsApp for stock updates.

communities.name: Oslo Debating Society

description.purpose: The University of Oslo's debating society. We train every Tuesday, run internal tournaments, and send teams to competitions in Norway and abroad, in both Norwegian and English (British Parliamentary format). Anyone can join, no experience needed.
description.culture: We're adopting a new constitution this semester, replacing the one from 1998 that nobody has read. The draft is in the Slack #constitution channel. Comment by the 15th, then it goes to a vote at the general meeting. Until then, the old board continues.

communities.notes: About 200 members, many of them passive. The new constitution would add equity officers and limit how long anyone can sit on the board, which veteran debaters see as aimed at them.

communities.name: Ruka Mapudungun

description.purpose:
Ruka Mapudungun ('house of the Mapuche language') is a circle for learning and revitalising Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche people. Many of our grandparents were punished for speaking it; many of our parents didn't pass it on to protect us. We're working to bring it back into our homes.

We meet in two ways:
- On Zoom, every Tuesday and Thursday evening, in groups by level. The beginners' group is led by young people who learned in recent years; the advanced conversation group is led by our elders (kimche), fluent speakers from communities in Araucanía.
- In person, in Santiago and Temuco, once a month, for a gathering with food, conversation and nütram (traditional conversation).

The WhatsApp group is for announcements, sharing words and phrases, recordings of elders (with their permission), and questions.

How we work:
- Elders guide the learning. Their knowledge of the language and its meaning comes first. When elders disagree about a word or a meaning, we accept that variation is part of the language; there are different ways of speaking in different territories.
- Classes are free. We ask those who can to contribute to cover the elders' travel and internet costs.
- Coordination is done by a small group of volunteers, chosen in a trawün (assembly) each year.

Rules:
- Respect the elders and the knowledge they share.
- Do not record, publish or share recordings of elders, ceremonies or sacred knowledge without explicit permission. Some knowledge is not for everyone.
- Non-Mapuche people are welcome to learn, with respect. The circle prioritises Mapuche participants when places are limited.
- No partisan politics in the group. Discussions about the territory and the rights of the Mapuche people are part of our life, but campaigns for parties are not allowed.

One thing we're discussing: which writing system to use. There are several alphabets for Mapudungun, with long-standing disagreements between them. Our elders mostly don't write the language, and some young people want to choose one alphabet for teaching. We've decided, for now, to accept all of them, and to keep listening.
description.culture: Patience, respect and joy. Every word we learn is a word that comes back home.

communities.notes: About 300 participants. Elders hold deep authority over the language; young volunteers do the organising. The rule prioritising Mapuche learners and the alphabet question both touch sensitive issues of identity and ownership.

communities.name: Grumpy Gardener Club

description.purpose: The Discord for listeners of The Grumpy Gardener, the podcast where a retired horticulturist complains about lawns, invasive species and Instagram gardening trends. Share your garden (he'll probably hate it), ask questions for the mailbag episodes, and swap seeds.
description.culture: Grumpy about plants, kind to people. Lawn defenders tolerated. No pesticide promotion in #organic.

communities.notes: About 2,000 members. The host's persona is cranky, but his team of three listener mods keeps the server gentle; some members imitate his grumpiness at each other and get warned.

communities.name: Ladder DAO

description.purpose: LDR: 100M fixed supply, 40% community, 20% treasury, 4-year vest, ve-staking for boosted yield and votes.

communities.notes: About 1,000 Discord members. The description is pure tokenomics: nothing about what the DAO does or how proposals work. In practice a core team posts proposals and holders rubber-stamp them.

communities.name: Noor's Bookshelf

description.purpose: My Discord for people who love books as much as I do. I post what I'm reading in Arabic and English, my notes, and quotes I underline. Friends and a few readers from my bookstagram hang out, recommend things, and we do buddy reads when we feel like it.
description.culture: No book snobbery. Romance and translated poetry are equally valid. Spoiler tags, please.

communities.notes: About 25 people, centred on a reader in Amman. Noor is the only admin; the buddy reads are organised whenever someone volunteers.

communities.name: Familia Gómez

description.purpose:
This is the family group of the Gómez family, children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren of Don Arturo and Doña Carmen. We use it to share news, photos, birthdays, and to organise the family meals at Grandma's house in Guadalajara.

RULES OF THE GROUP (from Grandma Carmen, written down by Lupita):
1. No politics. None. Not about elections, not about the government, not about other countries. We already had enough fights in 2018.
2. No religious arguments. Prayers and blessings yes; debates no.
3. No forwarded chain messages, fake news or 'share this or bad luck'. If you're not sure if it's true, don't send it.
4. No fights in the group. If you have a problem with someone, call them, or come to Sunday dinner and talk.
5. Good morning messages are allowed, but only one per person per day, please, my phone can't take it.
6. Respect the elders.

Grandma is the main admin. Lupita and Javier are admins too, to help with the phone. Anyone who breaks the rules gets a warning. The second time, they're removed for a week. Yes, this has happened, including to Uncle Beto.

What happened recently: Cousin Diego posted an article about the elections, and his sister answered, and in ten minutes there were forty messages and several people insulted. Grandma removed both of them for a week, and some of the family said she was being too strict and that adults should be able to talk about what's happening in the country. Grandma says the group is for family love, and that people can talk politics anywhere else. Some of the young ones made their own cousins' group where they can talk about anything. Grandma knows about it and has decided not to worry about it.
description.culture: This group is for family love. If you wouldn't say it at Grandma's table, don't write it here.

communities.notes: About 45 relatives across three generations. A family chat run with strict, written rules and real sanctions, enforced by the matriarch; the younger generation's breakaway group shows how far the strictness can stretch.

communities.name: KL Badminton Gang

description.purpose: Badminton every Wednesday night and Sunday morning in Cheras. Whoever books the court posts the slot here; first 12 to reply get in. Court fees and shuttlecock costs split equally, pay the booker by end of week.
description.culture: Fun games, not tournaments. Rotate partners so everyone plays with everyone. Don't hog the court for singles when people are waiting.

communities.notes: Twelve friends and former colleagues. Booking duty has drifted onto one person who always does it and is now often owed money.

communities.name: Rosemont Lane Tool Library

description.purpose: Borrow a drill, a ladder or a hedge trimmer from your neighbours instead of buying one. List what you can lend; ask for what you need.
description.culture: Return it clean, return it on time.

communities.notes: About 150 households on a Google Group. One retired neighbour keeps the shared spreadsheet and the shed key for the jointly bought tools.

communities.name: Line 4 Consultation

description.purpose: Public consultation on Line 4 of the Lima and Callao Metro, a 30 km underground line connecting the Port of Callao and the Jorge Chávez Airport with the east of the city, with 27 stations. Review the technical documents, the station locations, and the environmental impact study, and submit your observations through the form before the deadline. Observations will be answered in the final consultation report.

communities.notes: A formal government consultation portal. The description is entirely about the project; it says nothing about who decides, how observations are weighed, or the residents' groups along the route who are organising around displacement fears.
communities.setupNotes: government portal with a form; format unclear

communities.name: Night Desk

description.purpose:
Slack channel for the night desk at The Coastal Herald. The night team (two editors, three reporters, a web producer and a sub-editor) works from 4pm to 1am and puts out tomorrow's paper and the overnight website.

Handover: the day desk posts its handover in this channel by 4pm: what's running, what's developing, what's embargoed, what legal said. The night desk posts its handover to the morning team by 1am. Use the template. If it's not in the handover, the next shift doesn't know about it.

Corrections: if you spot an error in a published story, post it here immediately with the link and what's wrong. The night editor decides whether to correct online now or wait for the day desk. All corrections are logged in the corrections sheet. Nothing gets silently changed.

Legal: anything involving courts, allegations against named people, or children goes to the night editor before publishing. If in doubt, call the duty lawyer (number pinned).

Breaking news: the night editor decides what we chase. If you're called in after your shift, it counts as overtime, and you get the next shift late.

What we're working on: the last few months have been rough. After the newsroom cuts in the spring, the night desk went from eight people to seven while the website traffic targets went up. Two of us have been off with stress. We've asked the editor-in-chief for a change in how late stories are handled, and to stop expecting the night desk to cover breaking news and the print edition at the same time. In the meantime, we've agreed among ourselves: take your breaks, nobody stays past 1:30 unless the night editor asks, and it's ok to say 'I can't take that'.
description.culture: Sharp, fast, and honest about mistakes. Dark humour is a survival skill, not a policy. Look after each other.

communities.notes: Eight people working nights at a regional paper. The night editor has authority on the shift, but the real decisions (staffing, targets) are made by management who never see this channel. The team's own agreements are a quiet act of self-protection.

communities.name: Vet Nurses Australia

description.purpose: A group for qualified and student veterinary nurses and technicians across Australia. Discuss cases (anonymised), anaesthesia and nursing techniques, study for your Cert IV and diploma, share job openings, and talk about the reality of the job: pay, burnout, euthanasia, and difficult clients.
description.culture: Supportive, practical and professional. No naming clinics or vets in complaints. No clinical advice for pet owners; we're not a free vet. Look after yourself: compassion fatigue is real.

communities.notes: About 5,000 members on Facebook, run by three experienced vet nurses. Pay complaints are constant, and the admins are cautious after an employer threatened legal action over a post.

communities.name: Philosophy for Children, Grade 5

description.purpose: Our class's philosophy circle: we ask big questions and the class decides together how we'll talk about them.

communities.notes: 26 ten- and eleven-year-olds in Montevideo with a teacher trained in Philosophy for Children. The children write and vote on their own discussion rules and choose questions, but the teacher sets the classroom frame and safeguarding limits.

communities.name: Fare-Free Manchester

description.purpose: We campaign for free public transport across Greater Manchester, starting with buses for under-25s, over-60s and jobseekers, and building toward fare-free for all. We lobby the Mayor and councillors, run street stalls, publish research, and work with unions, students and disabled people's groups.
description.culture: Anyone who supports the goal is welcome. We meet monthly in Manchester city centre and online; decisions are made by consensus where possible, majority vote where not. Working groups handle research, comms and outreach.

communities.notes: About 1,500 on the mailing list, a core of 20. Allied unions and the student union bring people and money, and sometimes their own agendas.

communities.name: Vintage Synth Swap

description.purpose:
Vintage Synth Swap is a forum for buying, selling, trading and repairing vintage synthesizers, drum machines and electronic music gear: analogue polysynths, classic monosynths, early digital, modular, and everything in between. We also have sections for repair and restoration, history, and patches.

With about 9,000 members, a lot of money changes hands here, so we have rules for the marketplace. Please read them before you buy or sell.

Marketplace rules:
1. To sell, you need at least 30 posts in non-marketplace sections and an account at least 60 days old.
2. Every listing must include: clear photos (including one with a paper showing your username and the date), the price in your currency, location, whether you'll ship, and an honest description of condition, including faults and any mods or repairs.
3. After a sale, both buyer and seller leave feedback in the feedback thread. Your feedback score shows under your username.
4. Use a payment method with buyer protection for anything shipped. Never 'friends and family' payments with someone you don't know.
5. Price discussions in listings are allowed; public insults about prices are not. If you think it's overpriced, don't buy it.
6. Scammers are banned permanently and their details are posted in the Scam Alerts section.

Repair section rules: these instruments contain high voltages. Repair at your own risk, and take advice from people with experience.

Why so strict? In 2019, a member with good feedback sold more than 20 high-value synths that never existed and disappeared with about $60,000. After that, the admins introduced the current rules, and since then we've had very few scams.

The forum is run by its owner and six volunteer moderators. Moderators can remove listings and suspend marketplace access; bans are decided by the owner.

Current issue: prices for vintage gear have exploded in recent years, and some members are frustrated that dealers and flippers are using the marketplace to buy cheap from people who don't know the value and resell high. Proposals include limiting the number of listings per month, or requiring dealers to identify themselves. Discussion is open in the Site Feedback section.
description.culture: Gear nerds helping gear nerds. Share knowledge freely, trade honestly, and don't be a flipper.

communities.notes: A hobby forum whose culture is shaped by high-value trading and a past scam. The anti-flipper sentiment is strong, but some of the most knowledgeable and helpful members are also small dealers.

communities.name: Fieldnotes Wiki

description.purpose: Fieldnotes is a wiki where naturalists, hikers and researchers share detailed notes on places: trails, habitats, species seen, access, and how places change over time. Anyone can create or edit a page.
description.culture: Fieldnotes was started and run by one person (hi, it's Mariko) for nine years. This year it's becoming a nonprofit foundation with a board and community-elected stewards, so it's no longer dependent on me. The draft bylaws and steward election process are on the Meta pages. Please read them and comment.

communities.notes: About 800 active editors. Mariko has made every decision for nine years and is trying to hand over power, but many editors still defer to her, and early steward candidates are mostly her close friends.
communities.setupNotes: answered by founder for after the handover

communities.name: Bahá'í Study Circle

description.purpose: Study circle meeting on Saturday afternoons in Kilimani. Everyone is welcome, Bahá'í or not.

communities.notes: About 20 participants with a tutor who facilitates rather than teaches, following the Ruhi course materials. There's no clergy, so decisions about the circle are made by the participants themselves.

communities.name: Urban Heat Lab

description.purpose: Slack for the Urban Heat Lab. We study extreme heat in Phoenix: neighbourhood-level temperature mapping, heat illness among outdoor workers and unhoused residents, and cooling interventions. Channels for field campaigns (sensors, walking transects), data, community partners, and papers.
description.culture: Heat kills. Field safety rules apply: no fieldwork above 110°F without a buddy and the heat protocol. Respect our community partners; they're collaborators, not subjects.

communities.notes: About 16 people, with a PI and close ties to city government. Community partners are invited to some channels but feel peripheral to decisions about research questions.

communities.name: PM2.5 Kampala

description.purpose:
PM2.5 Kampala started in 2021 as a citizen science project. With help from a university team, about 60 volunteers installed low-cost air quality sensors at homes, schools and markets across Kampala, and the data went to a public dashboard. For the first time, residents could see that the air in Kawempe or Nakawa was often several times worse than WHO guidelines.

The sensor network still runs. Volunteers maintain the sensors, report faults, and help interpret the data for their neighbours. The university team checks data quality and publishes reports.

But over the last year, the group has changed. When people saw the numbers, they wanted action. Volunteers began organising: meetings with KCCA, petitions about burning at dumpsites, a campaign against the old diesel generators at the market, and in March, a march to City Hall, which got a lot of media attention and some arrests.

Now we're about 600 members in the WhatsApp community, and we're not sure what we are.

Some members (including many of the original volunteers and the university partners) feel the network's strength is that its data is neutral and trusted. They worry that if we're seen as activists, officials will dismiss the data, and the university may have to step back.

Others say data without action is useless, that the people breathing the air have the right to fight for clean air, and that 'neutral' too often means 'quiet'.

For now:
- The sensor network channel is for data, maintenance and technical questions only.
- The campaign channel is for organising actions. Participation is voluntary.
- The announcements channel is shared, and posts there must be agreed by the coordinating team, two people from the sensor side and two from the campaign side.

We're holding a meeting next month to decide whether to split into two groups, a citizen science network and a campaign, or to stay together as one.
description.culture: We breathe the same air. Facts first, but facts are for something. Respect each other across the disagreement.

communities.notes: A citizen science network that turned into a movement, now trying to be both. The university partner holds funding and data credibility; the campaigners hold the energy and numbers, and the shared coordinating team is a fragile truce.

communities.name: Nordlys

description.purpose: Norway's biggest hangout server. Chat, gaming, study rooms for upper secondary and university, county channels, music, memes, and events every weekend. Norwegian, Swedish and Danish all fine; English if you must.
description.culture: Be decent. No racism, no harassment, no NSFW. Staff are volunteers; respect them, and use the ticket system for complaints.

communities.notes: About 15,000 members, mostly teenagers. A large staff hierarchy run by an owner in his twenties; staff drama is a recurring issue, and staff turnover is high.

communities.name: Chronic Pain Coffee Morning

description.purpose: Coffee and chats for people living with chronic pain. First Saturday of the month, 11am, at the café on Oliver Plunkett Street.

communities.notes: About 80 people on Facebook, 10–15 at each coffee morning. One woman with fibromyalgia started it and does everything; there are no rules because nothing has ever gone wrong.

communities.name: Kooperatywa Spożywcza Warszawa (Warsaw Food Co-op)

description.purpose: A food co-op in Warsaw: we buy vegetables, grains, dairy and other products together directly from local farmers, at fair prices for them and for us. Orders are collected online every two weeks, and we sort and hand out the food on Saturday mornings in the community space on Grochowska.
description.culture: We have no president, no board and no officers, on purpose. Decisions are made at the open meeting on the last Thursday of the month by whoever comes. If you care about something, come and say so. Tasks (orders, contact with farmers, finances, Saturday shifts) are done by whoever volunteers, and swapped often so nobody becomes indispensable. If nobody does a task, it doesn't get done; that's how we learn what matters.

communities.notes: About 100 members. Deliberately officer-less, which keeps it egalitarian and resistant to capture, but the farmer relationships depend heavily on two people who 'happen' to always volunteer for them.

communities.name: Wellington Croquet Club

description.purpose:
The Wellington Croquet Club has played on its lawns in the Botanic Garden since 1911. We play both association croquet and golf croquet, socially and competitively, and host national and interclub tournaments. New players are always welcome; we have free coaching sessions on Saturday mornings, and equipment to borrow.

Lawns and bookings: we have three lawns. Lawn time is booked through the club website.
- Mornings on weekdays: social golf croquet, all welcome, no booking needed.
- Afternoons: bookings for competitive play and practice.
- Saturdays: coaching in the morning, club competitions in the afternoon.
- Sundays: open play.
During tournaments, lawns are reserved for the tournament.

Membership: annual subscription due 1 September. Members can book lawns, enter club competitions and vote at the AGM.

The club is run by a committee elected at the AGM in August: president, club captain, secretary, treasurer, lawns convenor, coaching coordinator and two committee members.

Etiquette: whites or light colours on the lawns for competitions. Flat-soled shoes only. Don't walk across a lawn where a game is in progress. Be generous with newcomers.

The ongoing discussion: in the last two years, golf croquet has grown hugely, with many younger and newer players, while association croquet, which has traditionally been the club's focus, has a smaller, older group of players. The golf croquet players say they don't get enough afternoon lawn time; the association players say golf croquet damages the lawns faster and that association croquet is the club's tradition and needs protecting. The committee (which still has a majority of association players) has proposed a new lawn allocation, which golf croquet players say doesn't go far enough. Expect a lively AGM.
description.culture: Sociable, sporting, and a touch old-fashioned in the best way. Tea is at 3:30 sharp.

communities.notes: About 110 members. Formal committee governance, but the committee's makeup lags behind who's actually playing, so the lawn allocation fight is really about generational control of the club.

communities.name: Second-Gen Koreans in Mexico

description.purpose: A space for people of Korean heritage who grew up in Mexico: children of immigrants, mixed families, adoptees. We talk about being 'too Mexican' for Korean relatives and 'too Korean' for everyone else, share food, hold meetups in Mexico City and Monterrey, and help each other with language, family and identity questions.
description.culture: No one has to prove they're 'Korean enough' or 'Mexican enough'. Spanish, Korean, English or any mix. Our parents' generation is welcome to follow along, but this space is for us.

communities.notes: About 400 members across Instagram and KakaoTalk, organised by three founders in their twenties. Adoptees sometimes feel the conversations assume a Korean-speaking family they never had.
