communities.name: The Long Field

description.purpose: My newsletter about rural life, land and slowness, now becoming a co-op owned by its readers. Details in the forum.

communities.notes: About 3,000 subscribers. The writer is handing ownership to a reader co-op where paying members would elect a board and could, in theory, overrule her editorial choices, and nobody is sure what that will mean in practice.

communities.name: Chorus Collective DAO

description.purpose: An independent musicians' collective organised as a DAO. Members release music together, pool streaming and sync royalties into a shared treasury, and vote on which projects get funding: recordings, tours, videos and gear. Each member holds one non-transferable membership token, so it's one musician, one vote.
description.culture: Artists first. We share the upside and the risk. Proposals are discussed openly for a week before voting. Support other members' releases. That's the deal.

communities.notes: About 300 musicians. Non-transferable tokens make it work more like a co-op than a typical DAO, but the treasury is dominated by royalties from three successful members, who are starting to question the equal split.

communities.name: Lena's Recovery Diary

description.purpose:
Hi, I'm Lena. I stopped drinking on 3 January 2023. I started this server as a diary: a place to post my day count and how I was feeling, where a few friends could see it and cheer me on. I didn't want to post it on Instagram, and I needed somewhere that wasn't just my own head.

Then my friend Ola asked if she could post her days too. Then her cousin. Then people I've never met. Now there are about 150 of us, mostly in Poland, some abroad, at different stages: some counting days, some counting years, some just thinking about it.

It's still my diary. My channel, #lena, is where I post every morning. But now everyone can have their own diary channel if they want, and there are shared channels:
- #check-in: post your count, or just 'still here'
- #hard-days: for cravings, slips, bad nights
- #wins: one month, one year, first sober wedding
- #off-topic: everything else

Things I ask:
- No judging anyone's path. AA, therapy, apps, medication, moderation, doing it alone: whatever helps you is welcome here.
- If someone slips, we don't lecture. We say welcome back.
- No sharing anything from here outside the server.
- This isn't a substitute for professional help. If you're in danger, or withdrawal is making you physically unwell, contact a doctor or emergency services. Links are pinned in #hard-days.

I'm not a counsellor or an expert. I'm just a person who's trying. Two friends, Ola and Marek, help me moderate.

I'll be honest: it's become a lot. Some days I feel responsible for people I don't know, and on my own bad days I don't have the strength to read #hard-days. I've been thinking about whether to hand it over, add more moderators, or close it to new people. For now I'm taking it one day at a time, like everything else.
description.culture: Gentle, honest, no shame. One day at a time, together.

communities.notes: Lena's personal diary that grew into a peer support community without anyone planning it. She's the founder and emotional centre, without training, and her own recovery is now tangled up with responsibility for 150 people.

communities.name: Tanaka Family

description.purpose: Our family group for the Tanakas in Osaka and São Paulo. Grandpa's brother emigrated to Brazil in 1958, and the two sides found each other again a few years ago. We share photos, birthdays and news, and we're planning a visit to Osaka next year.
description.culture: Japanese, Portuguese, and whatever the translate button gives us 😄. Be patient with each other's languages.

communities.notes: About 12 relatives reconnected across two countries. Communication relies on a bilingual cousin in São Paulo, who has become the unofficial organiser and translator.

communities.name: Brunch Club Accra

description.purpose: Nine of us, one brunch spot a month, honest reviews.

communities.notes: Nine friends in their late twenties. Picking the spot rotates; reviews get posted to a shared Instagram account that one member runs.

communities.name: Pasir Ris Residents

description.purpose: A community group for verified residents of Pasir Ris. Share local news, lost and found, recommendations for food and services, town council updates, and neighbourhood events.
description.culture: To join, you must answer the membership questions, including your block or street. Posts are approved by admins before they appear. No selling, no politics, no complaints about specific neighbours or businesses by name, no posts about race or religion. Admins may remove posts without explanation. Repeat offenders are removed. These rules keep the group safe and harmonious for everyone.

communities.notes: About 12,000 members, run by a few volunteer admins with very strict, pre-approved posting. Far more controlled than a typical neighbours' group; feels safe and orderly to many, overly censored to others who can't raise local problems.

communities.name: Tartu Youth Council Online

description.purpose:
The Tartu Youth Council is the elected voice of young people aged 14–26 in Tartu. We give opinions on city decisions that affect young people, propose our own projects, and run events. This Discord is where we work, and where any young person in Tartu can follow what we're doing and get involved.

Who we are: 15 members, elected every two years in an online election open to all young people living, studying or working in Tartu. Members elect a chair and two vice-chairs. We have a youth worker from the city who supports us, but doesn't vote.

How it works:
- Council meetings: twice a month, open to the public, in the city hall or online. Agendas are posted in #meetings a week ahead.
- Opinions: when the city asks for our opinion on a plan (like the new skatepark, school transport or the youth centre's budget), we discuss it in #open-discussion so any young person can contribute, then the council votes on our official opinion.
- Proposals: any young person can submit an idea in #ideas. If it gets 30 thumbs-up from Tartu youth, the council must discuss it at the next meeting.
- Working groups: education, environment, culture and events. Anyone can join.

Rules for the server:
- Respect each other, especially across languages: Estonian, Russian and English are all welcome.
- No party political campaigning. We're non-partisan.
- Personal attacks on council members, city officials or anyone else are removed.

The current situation: last spring, the city council approved plans to close the youth centre in Annelinn and merge it with the one in the centre, despite our formal opinion against it. Many young people felt ignored, and some asked what the point of the youth council is if the city doesn't listen. We organised a petition and a protest outside city hall, which some city officials thought was inappropriate for an official advisory body. We're now in talks with the deputy mayor about a formal agreement on how the city responds to our opinions.
description.culture: Serious about making change, not too serious about ourselves. Every young person's voice matters, not just the ones who are good at speeches.

communities.notes: About 300 on the Discord. An official advisory body that is formally part of the city structure, now caught between being consulted and protesting; Russian-speaking youth from Annelinn are under-represented on the council itself.

communities.name: Shree Textiles Floor Supervisors

description.purpose: Group for supervisors on all three shifts at the Shree Textiles weaving unit. Daily production targets from the manager, machine breakdowns, shift handovers, worker attendance and leave, and quality issues reported by the checking department.
description.culture: Keep messages short and clear. Report breakdowns immediately with the machine number. Shift handover message is compulsory before you leave. Personal matters, call directly.

communities.notes: About 30 supervisors and the production manager in a powerloom unit. Strictly top-down: the manager sets targets and supervisors pass pressure down to workers, who aren't in this group at all.

communities.name: Plumbers Who Code

description.purpose: Tradespeople learning to code, coders who got into a trade, and anyone building software for plumbers, sparkies and builders.
description.culture: No snobbery either way.

communities.notes: About 600 members on Discord. Part professional network for tradespeople, part hobby group for learning to code; tradespeople sometimes feel developers treat them as a market rather than as peers.

communities.name: Year 12 Chemistry

description.purpose: Teams class for Year 12 Chemistry, Ms Tupou. Notes, practicals, NCEA internal assessment deadlines and resources. Use the Questions channel for chemistry questions, and help each other out.
description.culture: Kia ora koutou, mālō e lelei. Be respectful, ask lots of questions, and don't share answers to internal assessments. Messages to Ms Tupou during school hours, please.

communities.notes: 26 students at a South Auckland secondary school. The teacher sets all the rules, and students mostly use their own Instagram group chat; the Questions channel is quiet unless an assessment is due.

communities.name: Mothers for Clean Rivers

description.purpose:
We are mothers from the neighbourhoods along the Buriganga and Turag rivers in Dhaka. Our children swim in, play near and drink water from rivers that have turned black with waste from tanneries, dyeing factories and the city. Our children get skin diseases, stomach illnesses, and worse. We came together in 2019 because we were tired of being told that nothing could be done.

What we do:
- Test the water. With help from a university chemistry department, our members collect samples every month from 20 points along the rivers, and we publish the results.
- Document. We record which factories are discharging, with photos and videos and dates.
- Pressure. We take our evidence to the Department of Environment, the city corporation, and the courts. We hold human chains and meetings.
- Educate. We go to schools and mosques and mothers' groups to explain the dangers and what families can do.

How we are organised: we have a group in each of the seven neighbourhoods we work in, each with an elected leader. The seven leaders form a committee, with a coordinator elected every year. Big decisions, such as legal action or national campaigns, are made at a general meeting of all members. We are supported by a small environmental NGO, which helps with legal advice and funding for the water testing, but the decisions are ours.

Facebook is for sharing our results, news and events with the public. Members also have private WhatsApp groups for each neighbourhood.

What we face: last year, after our evidence led the High Court to order two dyeing factories to stop discharging, some of our members received threats. One leader's husband was told he would lose his job at a factory if she continued. Some members have stepped back. We now keep the names of our samplers private, and leaders speak publicly only together, never alone. We are also discussing whether to work more closely with a national environmental organisation for protection, though some of us worry that a bigger organisation would take over our voice.
description.culture: We are mothers first. We speak with evidence and with love for our children. We stand together, so no one stands alone.

communities.notes: About 2,000 followers and a few hundred active members, mostly working-class women. A grassroots movement that has real legal successes and real risks, and a NGO partner whose influence is formally limited but practically significant.

communities.name: Speedcubing Uruguay

description.purpose: The community for speedcubers in Uruguay. Share times, algorithms and tips, organise meetups in Montevideo and the interior, and plan official competitions. Beginners to sub-10 solvers welcome.
description.culture: We used to be part of the big Río de la Plata server. We've set up our own space so we can organise Uruguayan competitions and meetups our own way. No hard feelings; many of us are still in both. Rules are simple: be friendly, help beginners, no cheating times.

communities.notes: About 250 members, mostly teens, who split from a larger Argentine-dominated server after a disagreement about where competitions were held. The new server's admins are still figuring out how to run things and occasionally ask the old server's admins for help.

communities.name: Tinyscript

description.purpose: A tiny embeddable scripting language in 2,000 lines of C.

communities.notes: About 30 contributors around a single author who reviews and merges everything personally. Feature requests are politely declined more often than not; keeping it tiny is the whole point.

communities.name: Kingston Prayer Line

description.purpose: A prayer line for believers in Kingston and the diaspora. Post your prayer requests: healing, work, family, travel, exams. Daily devotion and morning prayer voice note at 6am from Pastor Grant. Praise reports welcome!
description.culture: Bless and do not curse. Post prayer requests and testimonies only; no business promotion, no chain messages, no arguing about doctrine. Confidential matters, message the pastor privately.

communities.notes: About 400 members, admin is the pastor and his wife. Members from many churches, so doctrinal disagreements surface, and prayer requests sometimes reveal private family matters that people later regret sharing.

communities.name: Distributed Archaeology Lab

description.purpose:
The Distributed Archaeology Lab is a research group of about 20 archaeologists, mostly early-career, spread across universities and institutes in eight countries. We work together on the archaeology of the Bronze Age Mediterranean, with an emphasis on open data, field methods and re-analysis of legacy excavation archives.

We have no PI. That's on purpose.

We were founded in 2021 by postdocs who were tired of the traditional model, where one senior professor controls the funding, the data, the authorship and everyone's career. We wanted to try a research group run collectively, where everyone has an equal say, regardless of seniority.

How we work:
- Decisions: we make group decisions at a monthly call, by consensus. If we can't reach consensus after two calls, a two-thirds majority decides. Decisions about a specific project are made by the people working on it.
- Coordination: a coordinator, elected for six months at a time, runs the monthly calls, keeps the documents in order and is the contact for outside partners. The coordinator has no more authority than anyone else.
- Funding: grants are applied for by members, often as small teams. Because funders usually require a PI, whoever applies is the formal PI on paper, but by our agreement grant money supports the group's shared priorities, decided together.
- Data: all data produced by the group is shared within the group immediately, and published openly within two years.
- Authorship: anyone who contributes substantially to a paper is an author. We list authors alphabetically by default, with a contribution statement, unless a project agrees otherwise.
- Mentoring: students working with us have a mentoring team of two or three members, not a single supervisor.

We use Zulip for discussion (streams for each project, for methods, for grants, and for the group itself), and a shared repository for data.

The tension we're working on: two of our members recently won large individual grants, as formal PIs. Their institutions, and the funders, treat them as heads of their own projects and expect them to make decisions and manage staff. They've been honest that it's hard to honour our collective agreement when they're legally responsible for the money. We're discussing whether our agreement needs to change, and how to stay a collective as some of us become more senior.
description.culture: Collegial, open and a little idealistic. We argue a lot, and we think that's healthy. Everyone's ideas count, especially the ones from students.

communities.notes: A research lab deliberately without a PI, running on consensus and rotating coordination. It works, but its structure clashes with academic institutions that only recognise individual PIs, and success is now pulling it toward the hierarchy it was founded against.

communities.name: Azores Fluke ID

description.purpose: Help identify individual whales in the Azores from photos of their tail flukes. Whale-watching passengers, skippers and researchers upload photos, and volunteers match them against our catalogue of known sperm whales and humpbacks. Each match helps scientists understand migration, social groups and survival.
description.culture: Careful matching over fast matching. Double-check before you confirm. Credit the photographer always. Respect the whales: we don't support boats that get too close.

communities.notes: About 2,000 volunteers, coordinated by a marine research institute. Whale-watching companies provide most photos and get publicity in return, which makes the 'too close' rule awkward to enforce.

communities.name: Plaza Uno

description.purpose: Argentina's general forum since 2005. Football, politics, cars, tech, life.

communities.notes: About 45,000 accounts. Politics threads are notoriously heated and moderation is inconsistent; long-time users have far more leeway than newcomers.

communities.name: Young Widows Circle

description.purpose: A peer support group for people under 50 who have lost a spouse or partner. Monthly in-person meetings in Toronto, and this Facebook group for support between meetings.
description.culture: Since our facilitator Anne's position ended when the bereavement centre's funding was cut in June, the group has been run by members. We're still meeting, still here for each other. A few of us are coordinating for now; if you'd like to help, or have ideas for how we keep going, please share.

communities.notes: About 250 members. A professionally facilitated group that suddenly lost its facilitator; the members stepping in have no training and are grieving themselves, and the group is unsure whether to find new funding or stay member-run.

communities.name: Thiès Farmers' Cooperative

description.purpose:
The Thiès Farmers' Cooperative brings together about 900 farmers, men and women, from 30 villages in the Thiès region. We grow millet, groundnuts, cowpeas and vegetables, and through the cooperative we buy seeds and fertiliser together at better prices, share storage and a processing unit, get access to credit, and sell our harvest together to get a fair price.

How we communicate: most members don't read, so we use WhatsApp voice notes in Wolof and Serer, plus a monthly programme on the community radio where the president and the technical team give news and answer questions sent by phone. Each village has a relay (usually a young person with a smartphone) who passes information along.

How we are organised:
- Each village has a base group, which chooses its delegates.
- The general assembly of delegates meets twice a year, before planting and after harvest. It approves the accounts, sets the price policy, and elects the board.
- The board of nine members, elected for three years, manages the cooperative with a hired manager and two technicians. At least three board members must be women.
- Each member has one vote, whatever the size of their field.

Our rules:
- Members deliver at least half of their groundnut harvest to the cooperative.
- Credit for inputs is repaid at harvest. Members who don't repay can't get credit the next year.
- Disputes are settled first in the village, then by the board.

The current difficulty: last season, buyers from outside offered a higher price for groundnuts in cash, right at harvest time. Many members sold to them instead of delivering to the cooperative, and some didn't repay their credit. The cooperative couldn't meet its contract with the oil mill and lost money. At the last general assembly, there were hard words. Some want strict sanctions; others say members sold because they needed cash quickly and the cooperative pays too late. The board has proposed paying a cash advance at delivery, using a loan from the bank, and the delegates will decide at the next assembly.
description.culture: Unity is strength. We decide together, we respect our word, and we help each other through the bad years.

communities.notes: About 900 members with a strong formal democracy, voice notes and radio as the main channels, and village relays as gatekeepers of information. The side-selling crisis tests loyalty against members' urgent need for cash.

communities.name: Kandy Photographic Society

description.purpose: The photographic society of Kandy and the hill country. Monthly photo walks (temples, tea estates, markets, wildlife), competitions with judges, workshops on technique and editing, and an annual exhibition at the town hall. Share your photos in the group for feedback.
description.culture: All levels and all cameras, including phones. Feedback should be honest and kind. Ask permission before photographing people, especially at religious sites. No heavy manipulation in competition entries unless the category allows it.

communities.notes: About 500 members on Facebook, with an elected committee. Competition judging is dominated by a few senior photographers, and younger members who edit heavily feel penalised.

communities.name: Third Culture Kids Hangout

description.purpose: For anyone who's ever struggled to answer 'where are you from?'

communities.notes: About 3,000 members on Discord: diplomats' and missionaries' kids, military brats, children of migrants and expats. The identity is so loosely defined that members argue about who counts, and wealthier expat kids dominate the tone.

communities.name: Chef Rafa's Live Kitchen

description.purpose: The community for Chef Rafa's YouTube cooking lives! Every Wednesday and Saturday Rafa cooks live: Venezuelan classics, Latin street food, and whatever members vote for. Channel members get recipes in advance, a members-only cook-along each month, and access to the Discord. Share your versions of the recipes and cook together.
description.culture: In this kitchen everyone's welcome, even if you burn the arepas. Be kind in the comments and in the Discord. No politics, please; the kitchen is neutral territory.

communities.notes: About 6,000 members across YouTube memberships and Discord, many of them Venezuelan diaspora. The 'no politics' rule is hard to keep in a community bound together by migration, and mods delete heated exchanges almost every week.

communities.name: Ledger Library DAO

description.purpose:
Ledger Library DAO funds the creation, translation and maintenance of free, openly licensed textbooks for university and secondary school students, especially in subjects and languages that commercial publishers ignore. Since 2022 we've funded 46 textbooks in 11 languages, from introductory statistics in Swahili to organic chemistry in Bahasa Indonesia.

How it works:
- Authors, translators and teachers apply for grants through our proposal process.
- LIBR token holders govern the treasury and elect the people who run the grant program.
- All funded books must be published under CC BY, so anyone can use, adapt and translate them.

Governance:
- Delegates: most token holders delegate their votes to one of about 30 delegates, who must publish a statement of their priorities and explain their votes. Teachers and authors who've received grants are encouraged to become delegates.
- Grants Council: five members elected every six months review applications against published criteria and approve grants up to $25,000. Larger grants go to a full token vote.
- Educator Advisory Board: a group of teachers and librarians from the countries where our books are used. They advise the Grants Council on needs and quality. They have no formal vote, but the Council must respond in writing to their recommendations.
- Treasury: managed by a 4-of-7 multisig, with signers elected yearly.

Proposal process: post an idea in the Ideas category, discuss for at least a week, then submit a formal application or governance proposal using the templates.

Forum rules: be respectful, disclose conflicts of interest, and no token price talk.

Ongoing debate: the Educator Advisory Board has argued that because they have no vote, the people who know the most about what students need have the least power, while token holders, mostly crypto investors in Europe and North America, make the decisions. They've proposed giving the Board a formal veto over grants in their regions. Some delegates support it; others say it would undermine token holder governance and could slow grants down. A proposal is being drafted.
description.culture: Knowledge should be free. We fund generously, decide transparently, and listen to teachers.

communities.notes: About 1,200 token holders, maybe 100 active. The structure is careful and well-intentioned, but the gap between who holds tokens and who uses the books is the central governance question.

communities.name: Sela's Study Hall

description.purpose: My Discord for studying with friends. I made it during first year at uni in Auckland so my cousins back home in Tonga and my uni friends could keep each other accountable. We do Pomodoro sessions in the voice channels, post our goals for the day, and complain about assignments.
description.culture: Cameras optional. Studying only in the study rooms, chaos in #general. If you post a goal, someone will check on you 😤

communities.notes: About 30 people, Sela's friends and cousins in New Zealand and Tonga. She set it up and still decides everything, mostly by just doing it.

communities.name: The Pereiras

description.purpose: Pereira family group. News, photos and Sunday lunches.

communities.notes: About 25 relatives in Portugal, France and Switzerland. Grandmother doesn't use WhatsApp, so her daughter reads her the messages and replies on her behalf.

communities.name: Thursday Stokvel Sisters

description.purpose: Twelve friends, one stokvel. Every month each of us contributes R1,000, and each month one sister receives the full pot, in the order we drew at the start of the year. In December we also have a grocery stokvel for the festive season. And every Thursday we meet for tea, gossip and prayer at whoever's turn it is.
description.culture: Pay on time, no excuses: on the 25th, into Thandi's account, proof of payment in the group. If you can't pay, talk to the treasurer before, not after. What we share stays here. We're sisters first, but money is money.

communities.notes: Twelve women in Soweto and Johannesburg. A friend group that is also a rotating savings club with an elected treasurer and written rules; when one member fell behind on payments last year, the friendship and the finances got painfully tangled.

communities.name: Calle Luna 14 Owners' Community

description.purpose:
This is the WhatsApp group of the owners' community (comunidad de propietarios) of Calle Luna 14, Madrid: 24 flats and 2 commercial premises. The group is for notices, incidents in the building, and to coordinate with the administrator. It does not replace the general meeting, where decisions are legally made.

How the community works:
- The president is elected each year by rotation among the owners. This year it's Carmen, 3rd floor B.
- The building is managed by a professional administrator (contact details pinned), who handles accounts, contractors, insurance and legal matters.
- The ordinary general meeting is held once a year, in spring. Extraordinary meetings can be called by the president or by a quarter of the owners.
- Decisions are voted by owners according to their participation quota (it's in your deed). Some decisions need a simple majority, others three-fifths, and some unanimity.
- Tenants are welcome in the group for building notices, but voting is by owners only.

Group rules: notices and incidents only. No arguments: if there's a dispute, write to the president or the administrator. No commercial ads. Please be respectful; we're neighbours for many years.

The current topic: the lift. The lift is from 1968, breaks down almost every month, and doesn't meet current accessibility standards. The administrator has received three quotes to install a new one, the cheapest at €118,000, which would mean about €4,500 per flat, more for the top floors. Under the law, works to make the building accessible can be required if a disabled or elderly resident requests it and the cost doesn't exceed a certain amount; above that, it needs a majority. Several elderly residents, including Don Manuel (5th A, 89 years old), barely leave their homes. Some owners, especially those who rent out their flats or live on the ground floor, don't want to pay. There have been tense messages in the group, which the president has asked to stop. An extraordinary meeting will be held on 22 November to vote.
description.culture: Coexistence and respect. We share walls, stairs and, hopefully soon, a lift.

communities.notes: A building community with legally defined rules, voting by property quota, a rotating president and a professional administrator. The lift decision pits elderly residents' needs against absentee landlords' wallets, and tenants who are most affected can't vote.

communities.name: Open Budget Jakarta

description.purpose: We make the Jakarta provincial budget understandable for ordinary citizens. We turn hundreds of pages of budget documents into simple visualisations, highlight unusual spending, and help residents follow and submit input to the musrenbang (community development planning) process. Follow the website for analysis; join the Telegram for discussion and alerts.
description.culture: Evidence-based and non-partisan. We criticise budgets, not people. Corrections are welcome: if we got a number wrong, tell us and we'll fix it publicly.

communities.notes: About 1,500 members, run by a small team of volunteers with a data background. Officials sometimes engage, sometimes dismiss them; the Telegram attracts both citizens and partisan accounts, which strain the non-partisan rule.

communities.name: Hollowell & Co.

description.purpose: Commercial property, employment, private client and dispute resolution services for businesses and individuals across the South West.

communities.notes: This is the internal Teams space of a 70-person law firm, but the description is copied from the website. In reality it's hierarchical (partners, associates, trainees, support staff), with long-hours culture and a recent push from junior staff for flexible working.

communities.name: Iranian Engineers Abroad

description.purpose: A Telegram group for Iranian engineers living and working outside Iran, and those planning to emigrate. Share job opportunities, visa and work permit experiences, degree recognition processes, salaries in different countries, and professional advice. Sub-groups by field: civil, mechanical, electrical, software, petroleum.
description.culture: Professional and helpful. No politics; we have members of all views. No immigration agency advertising. Persian or English.

communities.notes: About 8,000 members. Admins, themselves engineers in Canada and Germany, keep politics out strictly because members inside Iran worry about their safety; this occasionally frustrates people who want to discuss events.

communities.name: Welding 102: Intermediate MIG & Stick

description.purpose:
Welcome to Welding 102. This course builds on Welding 101 and prepares you for the AWS D1.1 structural welding certification test. We meet Tuesday and Thursday evenings, 5:30–9:30, in the welding shop (Building C). This group chat and the course page are for schedule updates, assignments, and questions.

Shop safety rules (non-negotiable):
1. Full PPE in the shop at all times: helmet, safety glasses under the helmet, leather gloves, FR jacket or sleeves, leather boots, long pants with no frays. No synthetic clothing.
2. No one welds without the instructor in the shop.
3. Check your area for flammables before you strike an arc. Fire watch for 30 minutes after hot work.
4. Screens up when you weld. Warn people before you strike.
5. Report any injury, however small, right away.
Breaking a safety rule means you leave the shop for the day. Twice, and you'll meet with the program director.

Attendance: this is a hands-on course. More than three absences means you won't have enough booth time to be ready for the cert test. If you'll be absent, message me before class.

Grading: 60% practical (weld coupons graded on visual and bend tests), 25% written quizzes, 15% shop conduct and cleanup.

The chat: use it for course questions, carpools, and sharing job leads, there are a lot of them right now. Keep it respectful. We have students from 18 to 63 in this class, from all kinds of backgrounds; everyone is here to learn a trade.

Note from week 4: there was some trash talk in the chat about some students' welds. Constructive feedback is good: welders learn from each other. Mocking someone's work isn't. I've deleted those messages.

— Instructor Mike Delgado
description.culture: Safety first, quality second, speed third. Help the person next to you. Everyone's first bead looks like bird droppings.

communities.notes: About 20 adult students and one instructor with complete authority in the shop. The age and background mix (recent high school grads, laid-off factory workers, a retired accountant) makes the chat lively and occasionally tense.

communities.name: Ghost Nets Out

description.purpose: Fishers, divers and coastal communities in Palawan and the Visayas working together to remove abandoned 'ghost' fishing nets from reefs and beaches, and to stop them being dumped in the first place. We organise cleanup dives and beach days, recycle nets into products sold by local women's groups, and campaign for net-return programmes and enforcement against illegal dumping by commercial fleets.
description.culture: Small fishers aren't the enemy; they lose the most to ghost nets. Everyone is welcome at cleanups. Diving only with certified divers and the safety briefing. Campaign actions are decided by our coordinating team, with input from community leaders.

communities.notes: About 1,000 members. Both a volunteer cleanup group and a campaign; volunteers who come for dives are uneasy about campaigning against commercial fleets, some of which employ their relatives.

communities.name: Origami Tessellations

description.purpose: Folding repeating patterns from a single sheet. Share crease patterns, folds and questions.
description.culture: Credit designers.

communities.notes: About 2,500 members. Crediting the original designer of a pattern is taken very seriously, and posting someone's crease pattern without credit is the main reason people get warned.

communities.name: Bantu Lexicon Project

description.purpose: An open, collaborative dataset of words across Bantu languages, with forms, meanings, tone marking and reconstructed proto-forms, so researchers, teachers and speakers can compare languages and trace their history. Contribute data from your language, cite sources, or help clean and standardise entries.
description.culture: Speakers' knowledge matters as much as published dictionaries. Always record the source and the speaker's consent. Disagreements about transcription or tones are discussed on the issue tracker, with examples.

communities.notes: About 150 contributors, mostly linguists in Europe, the US and South Africa, with a growing number of speakers from East and Central Africa. The maintainers are academics, and speakers' corrections sometimes wait months for review.

communities.name: Mount Zion Congregation

description.purpose:
Welcome to the online home of Mount Zion Congregation. For 112 years, Mount Zion has been a church family in the heart of southwest Atlanta, and through civil rights, through urban change, through the pandemic, God has kept us. This Facebook group and our email list are where we share announcements, prayer requests, ministry news, and service times.

Services:
- 8:00 a.m. traditional service, with the Sanctuary Choir and hymns
- 11:00 a.m. contemporary service, with the praise team (starting January)
- Wednesday Bible study, 7:00 p.m., in person and on Zoom

A season of transition: as many of you know, our beloved Pastor Rev. Dr. James Whitfield, who has served Mount Zion for 34 years, will retire at the end of December. We give thanks for his faithful ministry. A Pastoral Search Committee, elected by the congregation in June, is leading the search for our next pastor according to our church's constitution. They'll present a candidate to the congregation for a vote, which requires a two-thirds majority. Until then, the Board of Deacons and Associate Pastor Rev. Lisa Monroe will guide the church.

We are also beginning a new contemporary service at 11:00, alongside the traditional 8:00 service. This was approved by the Board of Deacons after many conversations. We know this is a big change. Some of our longtime members feel the traditional service is the heart of Mount Zion, and worry that two services will divide the congregation. Many young families have said they need a worship style that speaks to them. We are trusting God to help us become one church in two services.

Group guidelines:
- Keep posts encouraging and related to church life.
- Prayer requests: share only what the person has agreed to share.
- Disagreements about church decisions should be brought to the deacons or the search committee, not debated in this group.
- No selling or political campaigning.
description.culture: A family of faith, rooted in tradition and open to what God is doing next. We honour our elders and make room for our children.

communities.notes: About 600 in the Facebook group. Leadership is in flux (retiring pastor, deacons, search committee, associate pastor) at the same moment as a service split, and the search becomes a proxy battle between traditional and contemporary factions.

communities.name: Quantum Optics Group

description.purpose: Workspace for the Quantum Optics Group. Channels for each experiment (entangled photon sources, atom trapping, integrated photonics), laser lab bookings, safety, group meeting on Fridays, and paper drafts. Lab manuals and SOPs are in the shared drive.
description.culture: Laser safety is everyone's responsibility. Never enter a lab with the warning light on without eye protection. Ask seniors before touching alignment. Share your failures in group meeting; they teach us more than successes.

communities.notes: About 19 people with a respected PI and a strict seniority culture in which PhD students rarely question postdocs. Lab time on the main laser setup is the biggest source of tension.

communities.name: Snow Depth Volunteers

description.purpose: Measure the snow in your yard every morning and report it. Helps forecasters and water managers across Alberta.

communities.notes: About 600 volunteers, many rural and retired. Run by a provincial agency with a coordinator who sends a newsletter; volunteers rarely interact with each other.

communities.name: Townsquare

description.purpose: Townsquare is a general social platform, like other social networks except for one thing: it's governed by its users. Post, follow, join groups, share whatever you like.
description.culture: Every year, members elect a Council of 15 people from among themselves. The Council writes the rules, appoints the moderation team, approves the budget and can overrule the company that runs the servers on anything to do with content policy. Proposals with support from 1% of active members go to a member-wide vote. The company handles engineering and money, and has agreed in writing not to override Council decisions on content. Read the charter before you post.

communities.notes: About 50,000 users. A large general social space that deliberately runs as a representative democracy; turnout in council elections is around 8%, and organised groups with specific agendas have an outsized effect on who gets elected.

communities.name: Parents of Autistic Children Lagos

description.purpose:
This is a support network for parents and caregivers of autistic children in Lagos and across Nigeria. Many of us were told our children were stubborn, possessed, cursed, or that it was our fault. Many of us waited years for a diagnosis, or never got one. We came together because nobody should go through this alone.

We have about 900 members, in a main WhatsApp group, smaller groups by area (Lekki, Ikeja, Surulere, Ikorodu, Abuja and diaspora), and a monthly meetup at a centre in Yaba where children can play while parents talk.

What we share:
- Where to get an assessment, and which doctors and therapists understand autism
- Schools that accept autistic children, and how to deal with schools that don't
- Therapy options and costs: speech, occupational, behavioural
- Daily life: feeding, sleep, toileting, meltdowns, communication
- Our feelings, our tiredness, and our joys

Rules:
1. Respect every family's choices and every child. No 'my method is the only way'.
2. No promotion of 'cures'. Autism is not a disease to be cured. Posts promoting miracle cures, deliverance sessions, special diets claiming to cure autism, or unproven treatments will be removed, and repeat posters will be removed from the group. You can share your experiences with therapies, with honesty about what they are.
3. No sharing children's photos or videos without their parents' consent, and never in a way that mocks or exposes them.
4. No selling without admin approval.
5. Be kind. Everyone here is carrying a lot.

The group was founded by Mrs. Adaeze Okonkwo, whose son was diagnosed in 2015. A team of six admin parents runs it with her, and a developmental paediatrician and a speech therapist volunteer as advisers who answer questions once a week.

The ongoing challenge: stigma. Many members are afraid to tell their families or churches. Some have been pressured to take their children for deliverance, or to hide them at home. Our admins remove posts that promote this, but some members feel we're disrespecting their faith. We try to hold both things: respect for faith, and protection of our children.

We've also had a few autistic adults join the group recently, who've challenged some of the language we use, like 'suffering from autism'. We're learning from them.
description.culture: No judgment, only support. Our children are not a curse; they are our children.

communities.notes: A strong, warm support community up against deep stigma. The 'no cures' rule puts it at odds with some members' faith practices, and autistic adults' participation is starting to shift whose voice defines the group.

communities.name: Riders Coop

description.purpose: We're a cooperative of delivery riders in Barcelona. Instead of working for platforms that pay us per order and can disconnect us whenever they want, we run our own: we deliver for local restaurants and shops, set our own rates and schedules, and share the income fairly. Telegram is for shifts, orders and the weekly assembly.
description.culture: Each rider-member has one vote. We decide rates, new clients and new members in assembly. Help each other on the street. Nobody rides alone at night if they don't want to.

communities.notes: About 120 riders, many migrants from Latin America and Pakistan. Earning less than on platforms during slow months strains loyalty, and the assembly is dominated by founders who speak Spanish fluently.

communities.name: Lisbon Fado Appreciation Society

description.purpose: Fado is the soul of Lisbon: saudade, the Portuguese guitar, and the voices of Alfama and Mouraria.

communities.notes: About 800 Facebook members. Actually a formal association with a board, monthly listening sessions and an annual festival; the description says nothing about any of that, and the group has quiet tension between traditionalists and fans of new fado styles.

communities.name: Assyrian Youth Network

description.purpose: Connecting young Assyrians in Sydney. We run Assyrian language classes, cultural nights, Kha b-Nisan (Assyrian New Year) celebrations, careers mentoring, and sports days, and we raise funds for Assyrian communities in Iraq and Syria. Instagram for events, WhatsApp for members.
description.culture: All Assyrians are welcome, whatever church or tribe your family comes from. Respect each other and our elders. Keep church disputes and politics out of the group.

communities.notes: About 700 members, with an elected youth committee. Differences between church denominations and political views on homeland issues simmer under the 'keep it out' rule.

communities.name: The Map Nerd

description.purpose:
Welcome to the Map Nerd Discord! This is the community for the YouTube channel where I (Tom) talk about maps, borders, geography, cartography, and weird places. There are about 25,000 of you here now, which is roughly the population of a small town. A small town entirely of map nerds.

What's here:
- #new-videos and #video-discussion: talk about the latest video, and point out what I got wrong (politely).
- #map-of-the-day: post an interesting map. One per person per day.
- #your-maps: share maps you've made.
- #geography-questions, #border-weirdness, #flags (yes, there's a flags channel; yes, it's chaos)
- #geoguessr: daily challenges and tournaments
- #community-projects: fan-run projects (see below)

Rules:
1. Be respectful. We have members from almost every country, and borders are personal for a lot of people.
2. No nationalist arguments, no territorial claims, no 'X is rightfully Y'. Discussing disputes factually is fine. Advocating for one side isn't.
3. No maps or content that glorify violence or genocide.
4. Don't post personal info about me or anyone else.
5. Moderators' decisions are final; appeals go through the ticket system.

Moderation: I don't moderate day to day. There are 14 moderators, led by head mods Priya and Gustavo, who were chosen from active community members. They have a private channel where they make decisions together, and they bring big questions to me.

Community projects: members run projects like the Fictional World Atlas, the Border Crossings Database, and the community wiki. Projects are led by members, with a mod as liaison.

What's going on: the Map Nerd Wiki, started by members in 2023, has become very popular, with thousands of articles. Recently, the wiki's founders decided to move it off the Discord's hosted platform to their own independent site, and to start showing ads to cover hosting costs. Some members felt it was the community's project, and that the founders shouldn't make that decision, or profit from it. The founders say they did most of the work and pay the bills. The mods have asked both sides to calm down, and I've said I'll support whatever arrangement the community and the wiki founders agree on. Discussion is in #wiki-future.
description.culture: Curious, nerdy and international. We love maps because they show us how big and strange the world is.

communities.notes: A large creator community that runs largely without the creator, through a mod team and member-led projects. The wiki dispute raises the question of who owns things a community builds together, and the creator is avoiding taking a side.

communities.name: Bridgefund DAO

description.purpose: Bridgefund is a DAO that pools funds and invests in early-stage crypto projects. Members contribute ETH, receive BRDG tokens proportionally, and vote on investments. Treasury managed by a 3-of-5 multisig.
description.culture: We're a tight crew. Proposals discussed in Discord, voted on Snapshot. Do your own research. Not financial advice.

communities.notes: Fifteen members who are actually a group of old friends from university. The formal DAO structure sits on top of a friend group; votes are formalities and real decisions happen in a group call, which makes it awkward when one member's investment pick loses money.

communities.name: Aziz's Vinyl Shelf

description.purpose: What's on the turntable today.

communities.notes: A Casablanca record collector's Instagram close friends list, about 40 people. Purely his space; friends reply in DMs.

communities.name: Johansson Summer House

description.purpose: The group for us who co-own the summer house on Orust, which Grandma and Grandpa left to their four children, now passed down to the 14 of us in the next generation. Booking weeks (shared spreadsheet), maintenance, the boat, costs and the annual work weekend in May.
description.culture: Book your weeks in the spreadsheet; summer weeks rotate between branches. Shared costs split by ownership share, transferred by 31 March. Bigger repairs decided at the work weekend, majority of shares. Leave the house as you'd like to find it, and don't touch Uncle Lars's fishing gear.

communities.notes: Fourteen cousins with unequal ownership shares in a family property. Family relationships and property rights collide; branches that use the house less resent paying equally, and a cousin who wants to sell her share has caused real distress.

communities.name: Old Boys of Form 4B

description.purpose:
This is the group for the boys of Form 4B, class of 1994, at our high school in Bulawayo. Thirty years later we're scattered: Bulawayo, Harare, Joburg, London, Leicester, Dallas, Perth. Some of us haven't seen each other since we wrote our O levels. This group keeps us connected.

What we use it for:
- News: births, weddings, new jobs, and sadly, funerals.
- The Funeral Fund. When one of us, or a parent, spouse or child of one of us, passes away, we contribute to support the family. Contributions are voluntary but expected: US$20 for those in Zimbabwe, US$50 or the equivalent for those outside. Mthunzi (in Bulawayo) is the treasurer and posts every contribution and payment in the group, with receipts.
- Reunions: we've had two, in 2014 and 2019, and we're planning the 30-year reunion in Bulawayo for December.
- Banter. Lots of banter. Football, mostly.

Rules (agreed after the 2020 incident):
1. No politics. We've lost friendships over politics. Zimbabwe politics, South African politics, British politics, American politics: take it elsewhere.
2. No tribalism. We were Ndebele, Shona, Kalanga, Tonga, white, coloured and Indian boys in one class and we were brothers. That doesn't change.
3. No forwarding of unverified news, especially about deaths.
4. Respect each other's families. No jokes about wives.
5. Admins (Mthunzi, Tendai and Gary) can remove anyone who breaks the rules after one warning.

About 2020: during the election arguments, two members exchanged insults that went too far, one about the other's tribe. Both were removed. One apologised and was readmitted after a few months. The other never came back. Some guys think we should invite him back for the 30-year reunion; others are still angry. The admins have said they'll reach out to him privately and see.
description.culture: Brothers from 4B. We tease each other mercilessly, and we show up when it counts.

communities.notes: About 30 men in their late forties across five countries. A friend group that also runs a mutual-aid fund with a treasurer and receipts; the 2020 removal still divides people, and the reunion forces the question.

communities.name: Seaview Road Elders Check-in

description.purpose: Neighbours on Seaview Road and the gap who look in on our elders who live alone. Every morning, each elder (or a family member) sends a quick 'good morning' in the group. If someone hasn't by 10, the neighbour assigned to them goes and knocks. We also share when someone needs groceries, a ride to the polyclinic, or help during a storm.
description.culture: Neighbourly, not nosy. Elders decide what help they want. Keep private health matters private. Everybody looks out for everybody.

communities.notes: About 40 people, half of them elders. Started by a retired nurse who assigns the buddies; it depends heavily on her, and she's in her seventies herself.

communities.name: Leuven Housing Jury

description.purpose: 24 randomly selected Leuven residents deliberate on affordable housing. Follow the jury and add your voice through our campaign.

communities.notes: The city set up the jury officially, but this website is run by the tenants' advocacy group that pushed for it. It blurs the line between an official civic process and a campaign around it, and jurors have complained it implies they share the campaign's views.
communities.setupNotes: could be movement; website doesn't fit formats well

communities.name: Kiosk Field Agents

description.purpose: Group for our mobile money agents and area supervisors in Dar es Salaam and the coast. Float top-up requests, system downtime alerts, fraud warnings, new rules from the company, and commission updates. Supervisors answer questions during working hours.
description.culture: Report fraud attempts immediately with the number and time. Never share your PIN, even with a supervisor. Keep messages professional. Commission complaints go privately to your supervisor.

communities.notes: About 200 independent agents who are not employees but depend on the company. Supervisors control float and commissions; agents rarely complain in the group for fear of losing their agency.

communities.name: Open Science Librarians

description.purpose:
Open Science Librarians (OSL) is a community of librarians, information professionals and researchers who support open access, open data, and open research practices in libraries and research institutions. We started in 2009 as a mailing list, and now include about 1,500 people across the list and our Slack workspace, from more than 50 countries.

What we do:
- Share knowledge and ask questions about open access policies, publishing agreements, research data management, repositories, copyright and licensing
- Run working groups on specific topics, which produce guides and toolkits
- Hold monthly webinars and an annual online 'unconference'
- Advocate collectively, for example by commenting on funder and government policies

How we're organised: OSL is not a formal organisation. There is a steering group of seven volunteers, chosen every two years by an open call and a vote of list members. The steering group manages the list and Slack, coordinates working groups and events, and represents OSL when needed. Working groups are open to anyone and choose their own leads.

Guidelines:
- Be respectful and assume good faith. Members work in very different contexts, from large research universities to small institutions with no budget.
- Vendor representatives are welcome as individuals, but no sales pitches or marketing. Disclose your affiliation if you work for a publisher or vendor.
- Share credit and cite work generously.
- Don't post confidential contract terms unless they're already public.

What's happening: last year, a major publisher offered to sponsor our annual unconference and provide paid speakers. The steering group accepted, thinking it would allow us to offer free registration to people from low-income countries. Many members objected strongly, saying a publisher with closed access practices shouldn't sponsor an open science community, and that it compromised our independence. The steering group apologised for not consulting more widely, returned the sponsorship, and has opened a consultation on a sponsorship policy. Draft options range from 'no sponsorship from commercial publishers' to 'sponsorship allowed with strict conditions'. The consultation closes at the end of the month, after which the steering group will put the options to a vote.
description.culture: Collegial, principled and practical. We share freely, because that's what we believe in.

communities.notes: A loose professional network with a light steering group. The sponsorship controversy exposed tension between principles and practical inclusion, and members from institutions with no budget were the ones the sponsorship was meant to help.

communities.name: Desert Willow Homeschool Co-op

description.purpose: A co-op for homeschooling families in Tucson. We meet Tuesdays and Thursdays at a church hall for group classes, from science labs and art to Spanish and PE, taught by parents. Families also organise field trips, park days and a spring showcase. The Facebook group is for schedules, class sign-ups and announcements.
description.culture: Every family teaches or helps in at least one class per semester. All homeschooling approaches welcome, secular or faith-based. Class decisions are made by the parents teaching them; co-op-wide decisions by the elected board of five parents.

communities.notes: About 40 families. Part school, part parent co-op: parents are both teachers and consumers. Secular and religious families coexist uneasily, and arguments about curriculum content flare up when a class touches evolution or history.

communities.name: Pedestrians First Hanoi

description.purpose: Sidewalks are for walking. Share photos of blocked sidewalks and push for walkable streets in Hanoi.

communities.notes: About 4,000 Facebook members, run by a few urban planning graduates. Posts shaming sidewalk vendors provoke heated debate, since vendors' livelihoods depend on that space.

communities.name: Kerala Aquarium Keepers

description.purpose: For fishkeepers in Kerala: freshwater, planted tanks, cichlids, bettas, native species. Ask about fish health, water parameters and setups, share your tanks, and buy, sell or exchange fish and plants with members in your district.
description.culture: Help beginners patiently. No selling wild-caught native fish from protected habitats. Sellers must post clear photos and prices. Disputes over sales go to the admins, whose decision is final.

communities.notes: About 2,500 members on Telegram. Several admins run local fish shops, which members say biases moderation of sales disputes.

communities.name: Shared Weather Archive

description.purpose:
The Shared Weather Archive (SWA) is an open archive of historical weather observations: digitised logbooks, old station records, ship observations and amateur weather station data going back to the 1700s. Volunteers transcribe handwritten records, researchers clean and quality-control the data, and the results are used for climate research, reanalysis, and local history.

Since 2016, SWA has been hosted and funded by a large technology company's research foundation, which paid for servers, two full-time engineers, and the transcription platform, and held the copyright to the platform code. The data itself has always been published under a CC BY licence.

What's changed: in August, the foundation announced it is ending its support at the end of the year. It has agreed to transfer the platform code under an open-source licence and to give the data and domain name to the community. But after that, there'll be no paid engineers, no server budget, and no one with formal responsibility for anything.

What we're doing:
- A transition group of nine people, including longtime volunteers, researchers who use the data, and one of the two engineers, has formed to plan what comes next.
- We're exploring three options: joining an existing scientific data organisation, which would provide hosting but would have its own rules; forming our own nonprofit foundation, which would need fundraising and a board; or splitting the archive between several university partners by region.
- We're also discussing whether to change the data licence to CC0, which some research partners prefer, and whether to require attribution of volunteer transcribers, which matters a lot to many volunteers.

How to take part: the transition discussion is in the Future of SWA category on the forum. The transition group posts weekly updates and will hold two open community calls before any decision. The aim is a decision by October, so that we have time to move the servers.

In the meantime: transcription continues as normal. Please keep going; every record you transcribe will be kept.
description.culture: Patient, careful and collaborative. Every logbook was written by someone who stood in the weather and wrote it down. We owe them accuracy.

communities.notes: About 300 core contributors and many casual transcribers. The sponsor's exit forces a community that never had to govern itself to decide its future quickly, and researchers' and volunteers' interests (licence, credit) don't fully align.

communities.name: Online Sangha

description.purpose: An online community practising meditation in the Theravada Buddhist tradition. We sit together on Zoom every morning and evening, hold weekly dhamma talks by visiting monks and lay teachers, and run month-long online retreats twice a year. Discord is for questions about practice, readings, and sharing retreat schedules.
description.culture: Practice with kindness, toward yourself and others. Questions about meditation are welcome; debates about which tradition is best are not. Teachers guide the practice; volunteers run everything else. Dana (giving) supports our teachers; give what you can.

communities.notes: About 300 members from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Europe and North America. Volunteers in the West run the logistics, while Asian members sometimes feel the community's practice has become 'meditation without Buddhism'.

communities.name: Neuroimaging Methods Lab

description.purpose: Lab Slack: MRI scanner bookings, analysis pipelines, code review, journal club.

communities.notes: About 25 people at a Montréal university with a PI who strongly supports open science; all code is public by default. Scanner time is booked months ahead and is the main source of conflict.

communities.name: Roadkill Reporters

description.purpose: Report animals killed on roads in Portugal and Spain: foxes, badgers, owls, hedgehogs, lynx, genets, snakes and more. Upload a photo and GPS location through the app. The most common species we record are hedgehogs, barn owls and common toads. The data helps identify roadkill hotspots and design wildlife crossings.

communities.notes: About 3,000 volunteers, coordinated by university researchers who validate every record and share hotspot maps with road authorities. The description is all species and nothing about who is involved or how; safety rules for stopping on roads exist but aren't mentioned.

communities.name: Pasar Malam

description.purpose:
Pasar Malam (night market) is the biggest Indonesian hangout server on Discord, with about 50,000 members. Like a real night market, there's a bit of everything: chat, gaming, music, anime, K-pop, study rooms, and regional channels from Aceh to Papua. Events every week: mabar (playing together), karaoke, quizzes, movie nights, and Ramadan and Independence Day specials.

Structure: the server is run by the owner (Raka) and a staff team of about 60 people, organised in a hierarchy:
- Admins (6): server policy, staff management, final decisions on bans
- Moderators (around 25): enforce rules in channels, handle reports
- Helpers (around 30): welcome new members, answer questions, run events
Staff are recruited through applications every three months. New staff have a one-month trial.

Rules:
1. Respect all members. No SARA (provocation based on ethnicity, religion, race or inter-group relations).
2. No NSFW content anywhere.
3. No spam, self-promotion or links to other servers without permission.
4. No buying/selling accounts or game items.
5. Use channels for their purpose.
6. Staff decisions are final; appeals through the ticket system.
Punishments go warning, then timeout, then kick, then ban, depending on severity.

What's been happening: in the last few months, the server has been hit by several raids, groups of accounts joining at once to spam offensive content, including SARA provocations during a sensitive period. The staff responded by adding verification (new members must wait 10 minutes and react to the rules) and phone verification for some channels. Raids have dropped, but many members, especially younger ones without their own phone, complain they can't access channels anymore. There's also been criticism that some moderators were too quick to ban members during the raids, including some innocent ones. The admin team is reviewing the ban appeals and considering a new rule that mods must get a second opinion before permanent bans.
description.culture: Ramai, seru, tapi tetap sopan: lively, fun, but still polite. Like a night market, everyone's welcome, but don't make trouble.

communities.notes: A huge, staff-heavy server with real hierarchy and procedures. Anti-raid security has traded openness for safety, and ban decisions made in a crisis are now under review.

communities.name: Burnout Recovery for Teachers

description.purpose: A Discord for teachers who are burnt out, recovering from burnout, on leave, or thinking about leaving. Talk about what happened, how you're coping, setting boundaries at school, and what comes next, whether that's going back, changing schools, or leaving teaching entirely.
description.culture: No guilt-tripping about 'the kids need you'. No shaming anyone for staying or leaving. Don't name schools or colleagues. This isn't therapy; crisis resources are pinned.

communities.notes: About 900 members, mostly in the UK, US and Australia, run by a former teacher and three volunteers. Some members want to organise collectively for better conditions; the founder wants to keep it a support space.

communities.name: Studio Nine Collective

description.purpose: Shared artists' studio in Glasgow. No members, only participants: whoever turns up and pitches in shapes what happens.

communities.notes: About 15 artists. Deliberately avoids membership, roles and formal decisions; it works because rent is covered by a small arts grant, and nobody knows what happens when the grant renewal needs someone to sign as the responsible person.

communities.name: Bucharest Cycling Club

description.purpose: Group rides from Bucharest every weekend: road rides to Snagov, Comana and the Danube, gravel in the forests around the city, and a beginners' ride on Sunday mornings. Routes and meeting points posted on Strava and in the WhatsApp group by Thursday.
description.culture: Helmets compulsory. No one gets dropped on the beginners' ride. On faster rides, read the pace in the description and be honest with yourself. Coffee stop is sacred.

communities.notes: About 300 members, organised informally by four ride leaders. The fast group and the social riders increasingly want different things, and the leaders are discussing splitting the group.

communities.name: Kinyarwanda Diaspora Parents

description.purpose:
We are Rwandan parents living in Belgium, Canada and elsewhere who want our children to speak Kinyarwanda and know where they come from. Many of our children understand a little but answer in French or English. Some don't understand at all. We came together to help each other.

What we do:
- Online Kinyarwanda classes for children aged 5–15, on Saturday mornings (European time) and Saturday afternoons (Canadian time), in three levels. Teachers are parents who were teachers in Rwanda, or trained volunteers.
- Story hours on Zoom, where grandparents in Rwanda tell stories, proverbs and riddles to the children.
- In-person gatherings in Brussels and Montréal for Umuganura (harvest festival) and other occasions, with traditional dance for the children.
- A WhatsApp group for parents to share resources, songs, books and advice.

How we're organised: a small coordinating team of six parents (three in Belgium, three in Canada), chosen at our annual online meeting. Class fees are low and cover teachers' small allowances and materials; families who can't pay are not turned away.

Guidelines:
- Speak to each other with respect, as Rwandans do.
- This group is for language and culture. We do not discuss politics, and we do not debate the history of our country in the group.
- Families have different experiences and different histories. We respect each family's story, and we never ask anyone about their family's past.
- Teachers will teach about Rwandan history in a way that is appropriate for children's ages, following the guidance the coordinating team agreed with parents. Questions about this should be discussed with the coordinating team privately.
- Photos of children are only shared with their parents' permission.

What we're discussing: older children, now teenagers, have started asking questions about history, including about 1994, that the classes don't answer, and some parents feel unprepared to answer at home. Some parents want the classes to address history more directly with older children; others feel this belongs in families, not in a language class. We're planning a parents' meeting, with the help of a Rwandan psychologist in Belgium, to talk about how we support our children with these questions.
description.culture: Patient, warm and respectful. Every word our children learn is a gift from those who came before.

communities.notes: About 200 families. A cultural and language community that carefully avoids history and politics because families carry very different experiences; teenagers' questions are pushing that careful silence to its limits.

communities.name: Cold Case Corner Forum

description.purpose: The official listener forum for Cold Case Corner, the podcast about unsolved cases. Discuss episodes, share research from public sources, and follow updates on cases we've covered.
description.culture: Victims were real people with families who may read this. Rules are strictly enforced: no speculation naming private individuals as suspects; no contacting victims' families, witnesses or police on the forum's behalf; no crime scene or autopsy images; no jokes about victims. Use the victim's name, not the killer's nickname. One warning, then a ban. If a family member asks us to remove a thread, we will, no questions asked.

communities.notes: About 10,000 members. A fan forum run with rules stricter than most professional spaces, because of earlier harm caused by amateur sleuthing on other forums. Some members feel it stifles legitimate discussion of evidence.

communities.name: Moonfarm DAO

description.purpose: Yield farming, auto-compounding vaults, MOON governance. LFG 🌙

communities.notes: About 700 Discord members, most of whom joined during a token airdrop and left. Anonymous core devs control upgrades; votes are rare.

communities.name: Elif's Dissertation Server

description.purpose: This started as my own server: a place to keep notes, post daily writing goals, and talk myself through my sociology dissertation. Then I invited two friends from my program for writing sprints. Now pretty much our whole cohort is here, plus some people from other departments. We do daily writing sessions, share sources, vent about supervisors (anonymously!), and celebrate submitted chapters.
description.culture: Since this isn't just my notebook anymore, I'm asking: what rules do we want? Suggestions in #how-we-run-this. Until then: be kind, protect each other's privacy, and no one has to share their word count.

communities.notes: About 40 graduate students in Ankara. A personal space turning into a cohort-wide community; Elif is still owner and isn't sure she wants to be in charge, and the supervisor-venting channel carries real risk if screenshots leak.
communities.setupNotes: started as personal; could be classroom

communities.name: Mum's Birthday Plot

description.purpose: Mum's 70th. Do not tell Mum.

communities.notes: Five siblings and one partner planning a surprise party. The eldest sister is in charge by default; the group will be deleted after the party.

communities.name: Pub Quiz Losers

description.purpose: Our pub quiz team. Tuesdays at the Crane, 9pm. Say if you're coming so we know whether we're a team of four or the full eight (max). Post your excuses for losing here.
description.culture: Nobody gets blamed for a wrong answer, except Niamh for the 2022 geography round. Phones away during the quiz. We don't cheat; we just lose with dignity.

communities.notes: Eight friends with a loose rotation. When more than eight want to come, nobody has the authority to decide who plays, which causes the only real friction.

communities.name: Plaine Verte Street Committee

description.purpose:
The Plaine Verte Street Committee brings together residents of the streets around the mosque and the market in Plaine Verte, Port Louis. We were formed in 2010 after flooding, when residents organised to clean the drains because nobody else would. Since then, we've become the link between residents and the Municipal Council.

What we do:
- Report problems to the Municipal Council and follow up: drains, rubbish collection, streetlights, roads, and stray dogs
- Organise cleaning days before the rainy season
- Help residents with paperwork and applications for social aid
- Organise neighbourhood events: Eid, Diwali, Christmas, and Independence Day, because our streets are mixed
- Keep watch on safety, together with the police station

How we're organised: each street elects a representative at a residents' meeting every two years. The representatives form the committee and choose a president, secretary and treasurer. The committee meets monthly, and residents can attend. Twice a year we hold a general meeting with the councillor of our ward and municipal officers, where residents can raise problems directly.

The WhatsApp group is for announcements, reporting problems, and sharing information. Please write in Creole, French or English.

Rules:
- No political party campaigning, especially before elections. The committee works with whoever is elected.
- No religious arguments. We are a mixed neighbourhood and proud of it.
- Report problems with location and photo.
- No personal insults against residents, committee members or officials.

The current issue: the Municipal Council has started treating the committee as its official partner for the neighbourhood, asking us to distribute information, choose which streets get repaired first, and even help select families for a housing programme. Some residents are pleased, saying we finally have influence. Others worry that the committee is becoming part of the council, and that we'll be blamed for decisions we don't control, or accused of favouring our friends. One of our representatives was accused of putting his relatives on the housing list, which he denies. We've agreed that from now on, the committee will not take part in selecting beneficiaries for anything, and will only pass on information and residents' concerns. We'll confirm this at the next general meeting.
description.culture: Our streets, our responsibility. We work together, whatever our religion or background, and we don't wait for others to fix things for us.

communities.notes: About 200 residents. Part neighbourhood self-help group, part semi-official liaison with local government; becoming the council's partner brings influence but also suspicion of favouritism, and the committee is redrawing its own boundaries.

communities.name: San Pedro Drinking Water Committee

description.purpose: The Drinking Water Committee of San Pedro manages our community's water system: the spring, the tank, the pipes, and the distribution schedule for about 300 households. We collect the monthly fee, organise tequio (community work days) to maintain the system, and represent the community in dealings with the municipality on water matters.
description.culture: Water belongs to the community. The committee is named by the community assembly every year, and committee service is unpaid and obligatory when it's your turn. Decisions about rates, new connections and repairs are made in assembly. Families that don't pay or don't participate in tequio may have their water cut, as the assembly has agreed.

communities.notes: About 300 households governed by traditional community practice (usos y costumbres). Committee members serve by rotation, without pay; migrants living in the US who send money instead of doing tequio are a growing source of debate.
